# AI usage

> The raw transcript is in `ai-sessions/`. It contains the OpenAI key from the assessment
> email, pasted into the session before I thought about it; it is redacted there.

## Setup

**Claude Code** (CLI, Opus 5, 1M context) for all of it — one session, no subagents, no MCP
servers, no custom skills, no `CLAUDE.md`. Everything the agent knew about this problem it
read out of `ASSESSMENT.md`, `data/README.md`, the 24 `.eml` files and `answer_key.json` at
the start of the session.

That was deliberate. The failure mode I was worried about was an agent confidently writing a
parser for emails it had never opened, so the first instruction was to read the whole package
and explain the problem back to me before proposing anything, and the second was to design the
architecture in prose before writing a line of code. Both of those outputs are in the
transcript ahead of the first file.

The one piece of tooling that mattered is not an agent feature at all: `scripts/score.py`,
written early, implementing the brief's metrics in the order it says it grades them. After
that existed, every change was judged by a number instead of by whether the diff looked
reasonable.

## How I worked

Deterministic layer first and verified with no model at all — all 24 emails ingested, every
attachment routed, the hidden Excel sheet skipped, the encrypted PDF flagged — so that when
model answers started arriving I knew the inputs were right. Then the scorer, then the model
layer. From there it was a loop: run, score, read the per-email diff, find the *cause* rather
than patch the symptom, fix, re-run. Five of those loops took dev from P 70.6% / 87 hallucinated
lines to P/R 100% with none.

I reviewed every diff. Two rules I kept to: a fix goes in the layer that owns the decision
(vague quantities became a code rule in `verify.py`, not another sentence in a prompt), and no
fix may name a string from the dev set — rules are about phenomena (hidden sheets, superseded
revisions, decorative images, bounce envelopes) because the held-out inbox has the same
situations in different words.

## Three moments

**It was wrong, and the scorer caught it — `0d8363a`.** Splitting tall scans into overlapping
strips fixed the quantity errors, so the agent added de-duplication by item number to remove
rows that appear in two strips. The next score run showed line recall had *fallen*: E010 lost
`40 | EA | 1/2"-13 hex nut, zinc`. That screenshot's first column is the quantity, not an item
number, and two different rows legitimately want 40 of something — so "duplicate item number"
had deleted a real line. The fix was to check whether the leading numbers form a contiguous
index before trusting them. I would not have found this by reading the diff; a net-positive
change hid a regression inside it, and only a per-line comparison against the key surfaced it.
This is the single strongest argument for having written the scorer first.

**I overruled it — `928bd5c` / `RUNNING.md`.** The key reached `gpt-5`, `gpt-5.4`, `gpt-5.5`
and more, and the obvious move was to default to the newest thing available. I said no, for a
reason that has nothing to do with quality: *they* run the held-out inbox with *their* key, and
if it cannot reach the model I named, the run dies. Defaults are pinned to the `gpt-4.1` family
— broadly available, and prices I can actually state in a cost report — with a fallback chain
for keys that cannot reach even those. The agent then tested the assumption I had implicitly
made, which was the better half of the exchange: on the scanned table that was failing,
`gpt-5` scored 14/28 and `gpt-4.1` scored 13/28. The newer model would have cost more, risked
the run, and fixed nothing.

**It saved me real time — `0d8363a`.** Ten quantities were wrong on E009's phone scan and I
would have spent an hour on image preprocessing — deskewing, upscaling, contrast. Instead the
agent proposed measuring four strategies against the answer key before changing anything:
full page, three overlapping strips, and two other models. That experiment took about four
minutes and returned an unambiguous answer (13/28 vs 28/28 vs 14/28) which both identified the
real mechanism — row drift over a tall table, not recognition — and ruled out the two
approaches I would have tried first.

**One more worth recording, because it is the test rather than the agent.** The resilience
inbox in `tests/test_resilience.py` failed on its first run, on a case neither of us had
designed for: an email with an empty subject, an empty body and one corrupt attachment comes
back classified `other`, and the output format forbids `needs_review` on `other`, so it leaves
with no lines and no flag. A silent loss produced by following the spec. That is now a code
override and it is written up in `DECISIONS.md` as my disagreement with the README. The agent
wrote the test; the test found the bug; neither the agent nor I had reasoned our way to it.

input.content:
# The matcher — designed, not built

Each extracted line has to become a catalog part, or a decision that Ridgeline doesn't stock
it. I did not build this; here is how I would, and why it is shaped the way it is.

## The shape the catalog hands you

`catalog.csv` is not a list of descriptions — it is already a structured table:
`category, product, size, spec, material, ends, extra, uom`, with 937 rows over 7 categories
and a closed vocabulary in every column (12 `ends` values, 22 `spec` values, `extra` is one of
nine). `description` is just an ERP rendering of those columns.

That settles the approach. **This is not a text-similarity problem.** Fuzzy-matching a
customer's sentence against an abbreviated ERP description is exactly how you quote the wrong
part, because the nearest string is routinely one attribute away from the right one. The job is
to parse the customer's free text into the *same schema the catalog already uses*, then compare
attributes exactly.

## The decision

1. **Normalise the line into catalog attributes.** From `description` (which the parser has
   already made self-contained) produce `{category, product, size, spec, material, ends, extra}`,
   using each column's own vocabulary — `Schedule 40`→`SCH 40`, `150 lb`/`Class 150`→`150#`,
   `butt weld`→`BW`, `threaded`/`NPT`→`THD`, `seamless`→`SMLS`, `1 1/2"`→`1-1/2`. Leave an
   attribute **absent** when the customer didn't state it. Absent is not a wildcard-with-a-guess;
   it is information about what they didn't pin down.

2. **Generate candidates** by exact index on `(product, size)` — a dictionary lookup, no
   scoring. `2" 90 elbow` gives 14 rows. Product names come from a synonym map onto the
   catalog's own `product` column (`ell`→`90 elbow`, `SPW`→`spiral wound gasket`, `WN`→`weld
   neck flange`, `T&C`→ends, not product).

3. **Filter by every attribute the customer DID state.** A stated attribute must agree exactly.
   Nothing is rounded, substituted or taken as "close enough".

4. **Decide by how many rows survive:**
   - exactly one → `matched`, that sku
   - more than one → `ambiguous`, `sku: null`, survivors in `candidates`
   - none → `not_in_catalog`, `sku: null`

The whole design is in step 4's symmetry: **silence widens the candidate set; it never narrows
it.** `1" WN 150# RF` names no material, and the catalog holds exactly one 1" 150# RF weld neck
(`RL-26367`, A105) — one survivor, so it matches, correctly, without anyone guessing a material.
Ask for `2" ball valve, threaded` and five rows survive on port and WOG rating and body
material; that is genuinely a question for the customer, not a coin flip.

## Why not-in-catalog has to be a real answer

Every one of the 16 non-matched lines in the dev key is one attribute away from something we
stock, which is exactly what makes substitution tempting and wrong:

| the customer asked for | what we stock | if you substituted |
|---|---|---|
| 14" weld neck flange, **150#** | 14" weld neck only in **300#** | wrong pressure class |
| 2" spiral wound, **316**/graphite, 300# | same size and class in **304** | wrong gasket material |
| 2" ball valve, **bronze, 125#** | 2" ball only in 304/316 SS at WOG ratings | wrong material and rating |
| **5/8" x 3-1/4"** B7 stud | 5/8" x 3" and 5/8" x **3-1/2"** | bolt that doesn't fit the flange |
| **eccentric** reducer 6" x 4" | **concentric** reducer only | wrong geometry for the line |
| **half** coupling 2" | full coupling only | wrong part |
| Y-strainer, hex head plug | not carried at all | — |

Three of those (material, class, length) would pass any string-similarity threshold loose
enough to be useful. So: no fallback, no "nearest part", no confidence score that lets a near
miss through. A `not_in_catalog` costs a buyer a phone call; a confident wrong sku costs a
rebuild.

## Where the model helps, and what it must never do

The model does **step 1 only** — reading a customer's prose into the attribute schema, which is
the same context-carrying judgement the parser already does well. It returns attributes, with
each one marked stated or absent.

The model never sees the catalog, never ranks candidates, and never names a sku. Steps 2–4 are
a dictionary lookup and a set intersection: deterministic, auditable, instantly re-runnable
when the catalog changes, and incapable of inventing `RL-31415`. If a model picks the part, a
wrong pick is unexplainable and unreproducible; if code picks it, `match_reason` writes itself —
*"2" 3000# A105 THD 90 elbow: one part fits"*, or *"14" weld neck 150#: we stock 14" weld neck
only in 300#"*.

One place I would let the model back in, read-only: when zero rows survive, ask it to name
*which attribute* caused it, so the reason line is useful to a rep. Its answer goes in the text,
never in the decision.

## How I'd measure it

The brief grades confident wrong matches first, so that is the headline: **a line where we named
a sku and the key says a different sku, `not_in_catalog`, or `ambiguous`.** Target zero; it is
the only matcher error that reaches a customer as a wrong quote. Then `not_in_catalog` recall
(of the 16 the key marks, how many did we decline to match), then plain accuracy, and
separately the `ambiguous` split — because the failure mode of a cautious matcher is flooding
reps with questions, and `ambiguous` on something a rep would call obvious is a real cost even
though the brief doesn't score it.

`scripts/score.py` already pairs our lines to the key's, so adding the matcher's three numbers
is a small extension of the same loop.

Two things I would watch on held-out data. Dev contains **no `ambiguous` lines at all** —
194 matched, 16 not-in-catalog — so my ambiguity rule is entirely untested and is the part most
likely to be wrong. And matching inherits every parser error upstream: a description missing its
schedule because a heading didn't carry becomes an ambiguity or a miss here, so matcher accuracy
is bounded above by the "context carried" number in `DECISIONS.md` and should be read alongside
it, never on its own.

| **half** coupling 2" | full coupling only | wrong part |
| Y-strainer, hex head plug | not carried at all | — |

Three of those (material, class, length) would pass any string-similarity threshold loose
enough to be useful. So: no fallback, no "nearest part", no confidence score that lets a near
miss through. A `not_in_catalog` costs a buyer a phone call; a confident wrong sku costs a
rebuild.

## Where the model helps, and what it must never do

The model does **step 1 only** — reading a customer's prose into the attribute schema, which is
the same context-carrying judgement the parser already does well. It returns attributes, with
each one marked stated or absent.

The model never sees the catalog, never ranks candidates, and never names a sku. Steps 2–4 are
a dictionary lookup and a set intersection: deterministic, auditable, instantly re-runnable
when the catalog changes, and incapable of inventing `RL-31415`. If a model picks the part, a
wrong pick is unexplainable and unreproducible; if code picks it, `match_reason` writes itself —
*"2" 3000# A105 THD 90 elbow: one part fits"*, or *"14" weld neck 150#: we stock 14" weld neck
only in 300#"*.

One place I would let the model back in, read-only: when zero rows survive, ask it to name
*which attribute* caused it, so the reason line is useful to a rep. Its answer goes in the text,
never in the decision.

## How I'd measure it

The brief grades confident wrong matches first, so that is the headline: **a line where we named
a sku and the key says a different sku, `not_in_catalog`, or `ambiguous`.** Target zero; it is
the only matcher error that reaches a customer as a wrong quote. Then `not_in_catalog` recall
(of the 16 the key marks, how many did we decline to match), then plain accuracy, and
separately the `ambiguous` split — because the failure mode of a cautious matcher is flooding
reps with questions, and `ambiguous` on something a rep would call obvious is a real cost even
though the brief doesn't score it.

`scripts/score.py` already pairs our lines to the key's, so adding the matcher's three numbers
is a small extension of the same loop.

Two things I would watch on held-out data. Dev contains **no `ambiguous` lines at all** —
194 matched, 16 not-in-catalog — so my ambiguity rule is entirely untested and is the part most
likely to be wrong. And matching inherits every parser error upstream: a description missing its
schedule because a heading didn't carry becomes an ambiguity or a miss here, so matcher accuracy
is bounded above by the "context carried" number in `DECISIONS.md` and should be read alongside
it, never on its own.

def default_cache() -> Path:
    """Where the recorded answers live.

    Installed with `pip install -e .` the package sits in the repo and REPO is right.

        if candidate.is_dir():
            return candidate
    return Path.cwd() / "cache"

"""The command.

    parse --emails <dir> --out parsed.json

Exit codes: 0 the run completed (flagged emails are a normal outcome, not a
failure), 2 the run completed but some emails could not reach a model, 1 the
run could not start at all.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import os
import sys
from pathlib import Path

from .pipeline import DEFAULT_CLASSIFY_MODEL, DEFAULT_EXTRACT_MODEL, DEFAULT_VISION_MODEL, run

REPO = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent


def _load_dotenv() -> None:
    """Read OPENAI_API_KEY from a .env beside the repo if the environment has none."""
    if os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"):
        return
    env = REPO / ".env"
    if not env.exists():
        return
    for line in env.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace").splitlines():
        line = line.strip()
        if not line or line.startswith("#") or "=" not in line:
            continue
        k, v = line.split("=", 1)
        os.environ.setdefault(k.strip(), v.strip().strip("'\""))


def build_parser() -> argparse.ArgumentParser:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="rfq", description=__doc__)
    sub = ap.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)

    p = sub.add_parser("parse", help="read an inbox of .eml files into parsed.json")
    p.add_argument("--emails", type=Path, required=True, help="directory of .eml files")
    p.add_argument("--out", type=Path, required=True, help="where to write parsed.json")
    p.add_argument("--cache", type=Path, default=REPO / "cache", help="recorded model answers")
    p.add_argument("--cost-report", type=Path, default=None, help="where to write the cost summary")
    p.add_argument("--traces", type=Path, default=None, help="directory for per-email traces")
    p.add_argument("--concurrency", type=int, default=6)
    p.add_argument("--refresh", action="store_true", help="ignore the cache and call the model again")
    p.add_argument("--no-cache-write", action="store_true", help="do not record new answers")
    p.add_argument("--model-classify", default=DEFAULT_CLASSIFY_MODEL)
    p.add_argument("--model-extract", default=DEFAULT_EXTRACT_MODEL)
    p.add_argument("--model-vision", default=DEFAULT_VISION_MODEL)
    p.add_argument("--quiet", action="store_true")
    return ap


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
    args = build_parser().parse_args(argv)
    if args.command != "parse":  # pragma: no cover
        return 1

    _load_dotenv()
    if not args.emails.is_dir():
        print(f"--emails: {args.emails} is not a directory", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1

    parsed, cost, results = run(
        args.emails,
        cache_dir=args.cache,
        api_key=os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"),
        models={
            "classify": args.model_classify,
            "extract": args.model_extract,
            "vision": args.model_vision,
        },
        concurrency=max(1, args.concurrency),
        refresh=args.refresh,
        write_cache=not args.no_cache_write,
    )

    args.out.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    args.out.write_text(json.dumps(parsed, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")

    report = args.cost_report or args.out.with_name(args.out.stem + ".cost.json")
    report.write_text(json.dumps(cost, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")

    if args.traces:
        args.traces.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        for r in results:
            (args.traces / f"{r.id}.json").write_text(
                json.dumps(r.trace(), indent=2, ensure_ascii=False, default=str) + "\n", encoding="utf-8"
            )

    degraded = [r.id for r in results if r.errors]
    if not args.quiet:
        flagged = [r.id for r in results if r.needs_review]
        lines = sum(len(v["line_items"]) for v in parsed.values())
        print(f"{len(parsed)} emails -> {args.out}  ({lines} line items)")
        cold = cost["cold_run"]
        print(
            f"  model calls {cost['model_calls']}, cache hits {cost['cache_hits']}, "
            f"${cost['cost_usd']:.4f} spent this run"
            + ("  [replayed from cache, no API key]" if cost["offline_replay"] else "")
        )
        print(
            f"  cold run would be {cold['prompt_tokens']:,} in / {cold['completion_tokens']:,} out tokens, "
            f"${cold['cost_usd']:.4f} (${cold['cost_per_email_usd']:.5f}/email)"
        )
        print(f"  needs_review: {len(flagged)}" + (f" ({', '.join(flagged)})" if flagged else ""))
        if degraded:
            print(f"  degraded (could not reach a model): {', '.join(degraded)}", file=sys.stderr)
        print(f"  cost report -> {report}")
    return 2 if degraded else 0

"""The command.

    parse --emails <dir> --out parsed.json

Exit codes: 0 the run completed (flagged emails are a normal outcome, not a
failure), 2 the run completed but some emails could not reach a model, 1 the
run could not start at all.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import os
import sys
from pathlib import Path

from .pipeline import DEFAULT_CLASSIFY_MODEL, DEFAULT_EXTRACT_MODEL, DEFAULT_VISION_MODEL, run

REPO = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent


def default_cache() -> Path:
    """Where the recorded answers live.

    Installed with `pip install -e .` the package sits in the repo and REPO is right.
    Installed without -e it sits in site-packages, where there is no cache — so the
    working directory wins when it has one.  Getting this wrong silently turns a
    keyless replay into 'no recorded answer for this input' on every email.
    """
    for candidate in (Path.cwd() / "cache", REPO / "cache"):
        if candidate.is_dir():
            return candidate
    return Path.cwd() / "cache"


def _load_dotenv() -> None:
    """Read OPENAI_API_KEY from a .env beside the repo if the environment has none."""
    if os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"):
        return
    env = REPO / ".env"
    if not env.exists():
        return
    for line in env.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace").splitlines():
        line = line.strip()
        if not line or line.startswith("#") or "=" not in line:
            continue
        k, v = line.split("=", 1)
        os.environ.setdefault(k.strip(), v.strip().strip("'\""))


def build_parser() -> argparse.ArgumentParser:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="rfq", description=__doc__)
    sub = ap.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)

    p = sub.add_parser("parse", help="read an inbox of .eml files into parsed.json")
    p.add_argument("--emails", type=Path, required=True, help="directory of .eml files")
    p.add_argument("--out", type=Path, required=True, help="where to write parsed.json")
    p.add_argument("--cache", type=Path, default=None, help="recorded model answers (default: ./cache, else the repo's)")
    p.add_argument("--cost-report", type=Path, default=None, help="where to write the cost summary")
    p.add_argument("--traces", type=Path, default=None, help="directory for per-email traces")
    p.add_argument("--concurrency", type=int, default=6)
    p.add_argument("--refresh", action="store_true", help="ignore the cache and call the model again")
    p.add_argument("--no-cache-write", action="store_true", help="do not record new answers")
    p.add_argument("--model-classify", default=DEFAULT_CLASSIFY_MODEL)
    p.add_argument("--model-extract", default=DEFAULT_EXTRACT_MODEL)
    p.add_argument("--model-vision", default=DEFAULT_VISION_MODEL)
    p.add_argument("--quiet", action="store_true")
    return ap


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
    args = build_parser().parse_args(argv)
    if args.command != "parse":  # pragma: no cover
        return 1

    _load_dotenv()
    if not args.emails.is_dir():
        print(f"--emails: {args.emails} is not a directory", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1

    parsed, cost, results = run(
        args.emails,
        cache_dir=args.cache or default_cache(),
        api_key=os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"),
        models={
            "classify": args.model_classify,
            "extract": args.model_extract,
            "vision": args.model_vision,
        },
        concurrency=max(1, args.concurrency),
        refresh=args.refresh,
        write_cache=not args.no_cache_write,
    )

    args.out.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    args.out.write_text(json.dumps(parsed, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")

    report = args.cost_report or args.out.with_name(args.out.stem + ".cost.json")
    report.write_text(json.dumps(cost, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")

    if args.traces:
        args.traces.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        for r in results:
            (args.traces / f"{r.id}.json").write_text(
                json.dumps(r.trace(), indent=2, ensure_ascii=False, default=str) + "\n", encoding="utf-8"
            )

    degraded = [r.id for r in results if r.errors]
    if not args.quiet:
        flagged = [r.id for r in results if r.needs_review]
        lines = sum(len(v["line_items"]) for v in parsed.values())
        print(f"{len(parsed)} emails -> {args.out}  ({lines} line items)")
        cold = cost["cold_run"]
        print(
            f"  model calls {cost['model_calls']}, cache hits {cost['cache_hits']}, "
            f"${cost['cost_usd']:.4f} spent this run"
            + ("  [replayed from cache, no API key]" if cost["offline_replay"] else "")
        )
        print(
            f"  cold run would be {cold['prompt_tokens']:,} in / {cold['completion_tokens']:,} out tokens, "
            f"${cold['cost_usd']:.4f} (${cold['cost_per_email_usd']:.5f}/email)"
        )
        print(f"  needs_review: {len(flagged)}" + (f" ({', '.join(flagged)})" if flagged else ""))
        if degraded:
            print(f"  degraded (could not reach a model): {', '.join(degraded)}", file=sys.stderr)
        print(f"  cost report -> {report}")
    return 2 if degraded else 0

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Copy this project's Claude Code transcripts into ai-sessions/, with keys redacted.

Run it LAST, just before sending — the session file keeps growing while you work.

    python scripts/export_sessions.py

It copies every .jsonl under ~/.claude/projects/<this-project>/ and replaces anything
that looks like an API key.  It then re-scans the output and refuses to finish if a
key-shaped string survived, so the check is not a matter of trusting the regex.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import re
import shutil
import sys
from pathlib import Path

REPO = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
OUT = REPO / "ai-sessions"

# OpenAI (sk-..., sk-proj-...), Anthropic (sk-ant-...), AWS, generic bearer tokens
PATTERNS = [
    (re.compile(r"sk-(?:proj-|ant-|live-|test-)?[A-Za-z0-9_\-]{16,}"), "[REDACTED-API-KEY]"),
    (re.compile(r"\bAKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}\b"), "[REDACTED-AWS-KEY]"),
    (re.compile(r"\bgh[pousr]_[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}\b"), "[REDACTED-GITHUB-TOKEN]"),
    (re.compile(r"(?i)\b(bearer)\s+[A-Za-z0-9._\-]{24,}"), r"\1 [REDACTED-TOKEN]"),
]
# anything key-shaped that must not survive the pass
LEFTOVER = re.compile(r"sk-[A-Za-z0-9_\-]{16,}|AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}|gh[pousr]_[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}")


def project_dir() -> Path:
    slug = str(REPO).replace("/", "-")
    return Path.home() / ".claude" / "projects" / slug


def main() -> int:
    src = project_dir()
    if not src.is_dir():
        print(f"no session directory at {src}", file=sys.stderr)
        print("if your tool cannot export, say so in AI_USAGE.md and bring the history to the interview.")
        return 1

    OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    files = sorted(src.glob("*.jsonl"))
    if not files:
        print(f"no .jsonl transcripts in {src}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1

    redactions = 0
    for f in files:
        text = f.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")
        for pat, repl in PATTERNS:
            text, n = pat.subn(repl, text)
            redactions += n
        dest = OUT / f.name

content.text:
Sharp question, and it's the right one. Let me answer it honestly, because there are two different things I did and only one of them transfers.

## Using the key as an oracle vs. as a detector

**Oracle:** "the key says 4, I said 6, make it say 4." That's fitting. It transfers nothing and it's why my 100% on dev should not be believed.

**Detector:** "the key says 4, I said 6 — *why?*" Then you find the mechanism, fix the mechanism, and throw the specific case away. What transfers is the mechanism fix. The key only told me *where to look*.

I tried to stay on the second side, but the honest test isn't my intention — it's whether each fix had a **key-free detector**. That is: could I have caught this on 40 emails I'll never see the answers to?

## Audit of what I actually changed

| fix | how the key found it | could I have found it with no key? |
|---|---|---|
| Scanned tables → strips | 10 wrong quantities | **Yes.** Item numbers 1…28 are printed in the table. If my output's numbers aren't a contiguous run, or a qty I return isn't in that column, the document contradicts me. |
| `rfq_revision` without a thread | 2 misclassifications | **Yes, logically.** You can't revise a message that doesn't exist. No In-Reply-To, no References, no quoted text → the label is impossible. No ground truth needed. |
| `needs_review` false positives | precision 0.18 | **Yes.** "I extracted 44 line items from this PDF" and "the items are in an attachment I can't see" are contradictory statements about the same email. |
| Item-number dedup deleting a real line | recall fell | **Yes.** I dropped a line as a duplicate whose text differed from the line it duplicated. That's a self-inconsistency in my own dedup. |
| "a couple caps" → qty 2 | 1 wrong qty | **Yes.** Already have the machinery — there's no digit and no number-word in the source. Asserting 2 is ungrounded. |
| E023 item counted twice | 1 extra line | **Yes.** The same item arrives from `body` and from the photo in one email. |
| **B006 silent loss** | — | **Found with no key at all**, by the resilience test. |

So six of seven have a key-free detector and one never needed the key. That's the defensible version of what happened. But — and this matters — **I only built two of those detectors.** Groundedness and the review-contradiction rule run in production. The other four exist in my head, which means on the held-out set they catch nothing.

That's the real gap in this submission, and it's exactly what your question is pointing at.

## How I'd actually work with no key

Replace the oracle with three things, in order of how much they're worth:

**1. Invariants the document checks for you.** The data audits itself if you ask it to:
- A numbered table's item numbers must form a contiguous run. Gap or repeat → flag.
- E005's spreadsheet literally says `TOTAL QTY | 35`. Sum my quantities. If they don't make 35, I misread something — **a free answer key, printed on the document.** Real BOMs carry line counts and totals constantly.
- A `qty` I return must appear in the source text (I have this; I only warn, I don't act).
- A line's size/schedule must appear in its own row or an ancestor heading — never invented.
- Flagged-and-complete, or complete-and-silent, are both contradictions.

**2. Self-consistency instead of ground truth.** On the expensive, error-prone documents — scans, photos — read twice with different framing (different strip boundaries) and compare. Agreement is cheap confidence; **disagreement is a review flag**. I don't need to know the right answer to know I'm unreliable here. That's roughly $0.02 extra on the ~15% of emails that are pictures, and it converts my worst failure mode from *silently wrong* into *flagged*, which is the whole point of the grading order.

**3. The rep is the real key.** In production nobody ships without a human in the loop at first. Every line a rep accepts or overturns in that web app is a label. Within two weeks you have a real answer key drawn from your actual mail, not from 24 synthetic examples — and the `needs_review` rate and the overturn rate become the metrics you actually run on.

And the discipline I *should* have used here and didn't: tune on half the dev set, measure on the other half. 24 emails felt too small to split, which is a reason and not a justification. The cheaper substitute is **perturbation** — mutate the dev emails in ways that preserve meaning (re-skew the scans, rename the section headings, change `SCH 40` to `Schedule 40`, reorder sheets, swap `jts` for `lengths`) and see which numbers move. Anything that falls apart was fitted. That's a held-out set I can manufacture today.

## What I'd do with the remaining time

Two things, both aimed squarely at the 40 emails rather than at the 24:

1. **Ship the invariants** — item-number contiguity, totals-row reconciliation, cross-source double-count, qty-not-in-source — as real checks that escalate to `needs_review` instead of living in my head. That directly converts silent wrongness into flagged wrongness, which is the metric they grade first.
2. **Build the perturbation harness** and report the numbers in `DECISIONS.md`. If my dev score survives renamed headings and re-skewed scans, the 100% means something. If it drops to 80%, I'd rather tell them that myself than have them discover it — and a candidate who reports their own generalization gap reads very differently from one who reports 100%.

Want me to build both? Roughly an hour, and (2) is the one that changes how your `DECISIONS.md` predictions read — right now they're my judgement; afterwards they'd be measurements.

content.text:
Here's the whole thing in plain words, then walked through each kind of file.

## The flow — six steps

```
.eml file
   │
1  OPEN THE ENVELOPE        who sent it, subject, date, body
   │                        split: what they wrote NOW  vs  the old thread below
   │
2  TURN EVERY ATTACHMENT    Excel / Word / CSV / PDF / photo
   INTO ONE OF TWO THINGS   →  text   or   picture
   │                        (or: "can't read this" — which is also an answer)
   │
3  WHAT KIND OF EMAIL?      one of 7 labels
   │                        ├── not a request? → STOP. Output empty list. Cheap.
   │                        └── a request? → carry on
   │
4  READ EACH DOCUMENT       one AI call per document
   │                        "give me the line items in THIS document"
   │
5  CHECK EVERY LINE         does this line really exist in that document?
   │                        is the unit a real unit? is the qty sane?
   │                        → lines that fail get thrown away
   │
6  LOOK AT THE WHOLE INBOX  is this a duplicate? a revision of an earlier email?
   │                        did anything fail to read? → flag for a human
   │
parsed.json
```

Step 5 is the important one. The AI *suggests* lines; the code *decides* which ones ship.

---

## What each file type does in step 2

| what arrives | what we do | result |
|---|---|---|
| plain text body | use it as-is | text |
| HTML body with a table | convert table rows to `cell \| cell \| cell` | text |
| **CSV** | read rows, join with `\|` | text |
| **Excel** | read each sheet, **skip hidden sheets**, put the tab name at the top | text |
| **Word** | paragraphs + table rows, keep the headings | text |
| **PDF with real text** | rebuild the table columns from word positions | text |
| **PDF that's a scan** | no text inside → render pages as images | picture |
| **photo / screenshot** | pass through | picture |
| **encrypted / corrupt / .xls** | can't open | "can't read" |
| **an email attached to an email** | read it, but tag whose it is | text |

We decide by **looking at the bytes**, not the file name. A file called `list.xlsx` that's really a CSV still gets read correctly.

---

## Worked examples

### 1. Text only — E001

Body is a plain list:

```
12 jts - 2" SCH 40 A53B ERW black pipe, PE
...
4" 150# RF slip-on flange, A105 x 6
```

No attachments. Classified `rfq`. One AI call on the body → 5 lines.

Note the last line: the quantity is at the **end** (`x 6`), not the front. And the signature block, phone number and confidentiality notice below are *not* lines. That's why even "easy" emails go through the model.

### 2. Text with headings — E003 (the context test)

```
All pipe SCH 40 A53B ERW, T&C.      ← applies to the PIPE section only

PIPE
1) 20 jts - 2"
2) 10 jts - 3"

FITTINGS - fittings are 150# malleable iron, black   ← applies here only
4) 12 ea - 2" 90 ell
```

Line 1 ships as `2" pipe, SCH 40 A53B ERW, threaded & coupled`.
Line 4 ships as `2" 90 elbow, 150# malleable iron, black` — **and must not say SCH 40.**

Carrying the heading down to the right lines, and *not* to the wrong ones, is the main skill being graded.

### 3. CSV — E016 (and it's a forward)

The email is from `marcus.doyle@ridgeline-supply.example` — that's **our own rep** forwarding a customer. So we classify it as the *customer's* email (`rfq`), and we read the forwarded text too.

Attached CSV:
```
Qty,UOM,Size,Description
60,FT,"1-1/2""","Pipe, SCH 80, A106B SMLS, PE"
```
becomes
```
60 | FT | 1-1/2" | Pipe, SCH 80, A106B SMLS, PE
```
→ 6 lines, `source: "HM-7716_material_list.csv"`.

### 4. Excel — E005 (the hidden sheet)

The workbook has two tabs:
- `Rev B` — visible
- `Rev A (old)` — **hidden**, with different quantities

We skip hidden sheets entirely. Then the visible sheet reads:

```
=== SHEET: Rev B ===
Gulf Terminals - Tank 14 Piping Modifications - Bid 26-0412
ALL FITTINGS BW SCH 40 A234 WPB UNLESS NOTED      ← a default for every row
ITEM | QTY | UOM | SIZE | DESCRIPTION             ← column header, not a line
90 ELBOWS                                          ← section title, not a line
1 | 12 | EA | 6" | 90 LR elbow
...
6 | 2 | EA | 6" x 4" | Reducer, concentric, SCH 80   ← says SCH 80 itself
 | TOTAL QTY | 35                                  ← totals row, not a line
```

Row 6 **overrides** the default — it ships as SCH 80 and must *not* mention SCH 40. Rows 1–5, 7, 8 inherit SCH 40.

### 5. Excel, two tabs — E021

```
=== SHEET: PIPE - SCH 80 SMLS ===
1 | 420 | FT | 1/2" | PE

=== SHEET: FITTINGS - SW 3000# ===
1 | 9 | EA | 1/2" | 90 Elbow
```

The spec is **in the tab name**. 50 lines, each one carrying its own tab's spec. Both tabs restart numbering at `1` — which is why our duplicate-removal doesn't just trust leading numbers (more on that below).

### 6. PDF with real text — E006

The PDF is a proper RFQ form. We rebuild the columns from word positions:

```
RFQ No.: | PF-26-3091 | Required By: | 10/22/2026
Material: | ASTM A105       ← a form field — context for every row
Rating: | 150# RF
ITEM | QTY | UOM | SIZE | DESCRIPTION
1 | 7 | EA | 1/2" | WELD NECK FLANGE, STD BORE
```
→ 44 lines from the PDF.

**Plus** the email body says "Also please add: 2 sets of 4" gaskets, 6 sets of 6" gaskets" → 2 more lines with `source: "body"`.

So one email, **two sources**, 46 lines.

And this is where step 5 proved itself: when reading the PDF, the AI also tried to return those two gasket lines (it can see the body as background context). The code checked — *are those words actually in the PDF?* No → **dropped**. Without that check we'd have quoted the gaskets twice.

### 7. Scanned PDF — E009 (the one that needed real work)

The PDF has no text inside — it's a phone photo of a form, 2 pages, 32 items. So we render it as pictures.

First attempt: send the whole page → the AI read **13 of 28 quantities correctly**. It was sliding between rows — pairing row 3's quantity with row 4's size.

The fix wasn't a bigger AI. We tested that: `gpt-5` on the whole page got 14/28. Instead we **cut each page into 3 overlapping horizontal strips** and read each strip:

```
┌─────────────┐
│  strip 1    │  rows 1-10
├─────────────┤  (overlap)
│  strip 2    │  rows 9-19
├─────────────┤  (overlap)
│  strip 3    │  rows 18-28
└─────────────┘
```

→ **28 of 28.** Fewer rows in one look = no drifting.

Two knock-on problems the strips created, both fixed:
- **Overlap repeats rows.** We remove repeats by item number — but only when the leading numbers look like a real index (1,2,3…). In E010 the first column is the *quantity* and two rows both say `40`, so blindly removing "duplicates" deleted a real line. Now we check first.
- **Page 2 lost its heading.** Items 29–32 are stud bolts, but "STUD BOLTS" is printed back on page 1. So each page now gets handed a summary of the last few rows read, and continues the section.

### 8. Phone photo of a handwritten list — E007

```
8 - 2" galv 90 elbow
4 - ,, tee                    ← ditto marks = 2" galv
6 - 1" x 3" galv nipple
6 - 1" x 4" ,,                ← ditto = galv nipple
3 - 3/4" bronze ball valve    ← CROSSED OUT — customer deleted it
12 - 2" galv coupling
```

7 lines out, not 8. The struck-through line is a deletion, and the ditto marks get resolved from the line above. Note: plain OCR can't see a strikethrough — you need something that actually *looks* at the image.

### 9. Photo of a nameplate — E023 (quantity and spec live apart)

Body: *"can you quote 3 of these, same as the one in the pic"*
Photo: a valve tag reading `HALVORSEN VALVE CO. / GATE VALVE / MODEL: HV-800-FGS / SIZE: 2 IN / CLASS: 800 LB / ENDS: NPT / BODY: A105 / TRIM: 13CR`

Result: **one** line. Quantity `3` comes from the body, the whole specification comes from the photo, and `source` is the photo.

This is why every document call also gets the email body as background — and why step 5 then enforces "the line itself must be in this document."

### 10. Pasted screenshot — E010 (the size trap)

Two inline images:
- `image001.png` — **3,307 bytes** — company logo
- `image002.png` — **4,295 bytes** — screenshot of a spreadsheet with 6 real line items

The logo is *smaller* than the real content. (And in E017 the logo is 5,288 bytes — bigger than both.) So we never judge by file size. Every image goes to the AI, and **"this is just a logo"** is an allowed answer.

### 11. HTML table — E024

The plain-text version flattens the table. The HTML version has the spec in a merged header cell:

```
316 SS – THREADED – 3000#      ← spans all 3 columns
Qty | Description | Size
10  | 90° elbow   | 1/2″
```

So when an email has an HTML table, we use the HTML. Every description carries `316 SS, threaded, 3000#`.

### 12. Pasted table that lost its shape — E018

Someone copied from Excel and the columns collapsed into separate lines:

```
8
Weld neck flange, 150# RF, A105, STD bore
4"
12
90 deg elbow, LR, BW, SCH 40, A234 WPB
4"
```

The AI stitches them back: `8 × 4" weld neck flange, 150# RF, A105`. Also `12 rolls` → unit `RL`.

---

## The emails that look like requests but aren't

These all come back with **zero lines** — and getting that right is worth as much as extracting correctly.

| email | what it looks like | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| **E011** | a neat list of 4 items with quantities | a **supplier quoting us** — has prices, lead times, FOB terms, and it's replying to our own rep → `vendor_quote` |
| **E012** | a full 7-line RFQ in the body | that RFQ is **quoted history** from 3 weeks ago; the actual message is "any update?" → `status_inquiry` |
| **E013** | contains a complete 4-item order | a **bounce notice** carrying *our own outbound* email → `auto_reply` |
| **E014** | a price table of flanges | a **marketing blast** → `other` |

The main defence: **quoted history is never shown to the extractor at all.** Not labelled "ignore this" — simply not included. It can't hallucinate what it never saw.

---

## Threads and repeats

**E003 → E004 (a revision).** The reply says: *"Line 2 is now 14 jts. Drop the unions. Add 4 ea 2" ball valves."*

We take E003's 8 recorded lines, apply the three changes, and output the **complete order as it now stands** — 8 lines, with the union gone and the ball valve added. E003 keeps its original 8 lines untouched. `revises: "E003"`.

**E006 → E008 (a duplicate).** Same customer, subject `RESEND: RFQ PF-26-3091` vs `RFQ PF-26-3091`, **byte-identical PDF attached**. The later one is the duplicate → `duplicate_of: "E006"`, zero lines. (The covering note was rewritten, so matching the body text wouldn't have caught it — the attachment hash did.)

---

## When we can't read it

| email | problem | what we do |
|---|---|---|
| **E017** | says "BOM attached" — the only attachment is the **company logo** | `needs_review: true`, zero lines, reason says so |
| **E022** | PDF is **password-protected** ("password to follow separately") | `needs_review: true` |

This is the single most important behaviour. Returning an empty list with no flag means a customer emailed and **nobody ever replied**. The brief ranks that as the worst possible failure, above getting lines wrong.

So the rule is: *if you can't read it, say you can't read it.* Never go quiet.

---

## And the money

Because step 3 stops early on non-requests:

- E011, E012, E013, E014 → **$0.0007 each** (one cheap classification call, nothing else)
- E009 (32-line scan) → $0.0380
- E006 (44-line PDF) → $0.0332
- **Whole dev inbox: $0.29 for 24 emails** — and **$0.00** the second time, because every answer is saved to disk.

Here it is as pure input → output, step by step.

---

## Step 1 — Open the envelope

**IN:** one `.eml` file (raw bytes)

**OUT:** a structured record

```
id:          "E006"
from:        mdubois@pelicanfab.example
date:        2026-10-08 09:14
subject:     "RFQ PF-26-3091 flanges"
body_now:    "Hi team, RFQ attached... Also please add: 2 sets of 4" gaskets..."
body_quoted: ""                       ← the old thread below, kept separate
attachments: [ RFQ_PF-26-3091.pdf (4927 bytes) ]
```

The key output is that **`body_now` and `body_quoted` are two different fields.**

---

## Step 2 — Turn attachments into documents

**IN:** the attachment bytes

**OUT:** a list of documents, each with a name and either text or pictures

```
[
  { source: "body",                 kind: text,    text: "Hi team, RFQ attached..." },
  { source: "RFQ_PF-26-3091.pdf",   kind: text,    text: "ITEM | QTY | UOM | ..." }
]
```

Three possible `kind` values:

| kind | when | example |
|---|---|---|
| `text` | Excel, Word, CSV, PDF-with-text, HTML | E006 PDF, E016 CSV |
| `picture` | photo, screenshot, scanned PDF | E009 scan, E007 photo |
| `unreadable` | encrypted, corrupt, .xls | E022 password PDF |

---

## Step 3 — What kind of email?

**IN:** headers + `body_now` + a short preview of each document

**OUT:** one label

```
classification: "rfq"
carries_items:  true
```

**This is a gate:**

```
rfq / rfq_revision / purchase_order   →  go to step 4
vendor_quote / status_inquiry
  / auto_reply / other                →  STOP. line_items = []
```

Stopping here is why E011, E012, E013, E014 each cost $0.0007 instead of $0.03.

---

## Step 4 — Read each document

**IN:** ONE document + the email's subject and body as background

**OUT:** suggested lines from that one document

For `RFQ_PF-26-3091.pdf`:
```
[
  { raw: "1 | 7 | EA | 1/2\" | WELD NECK FLANGE, STD BORE",
    description: "1/2\" weld neck flange, 150# RF, A105, STD bore",
    qty: 7, uom: "EA" },
  ... 43 more
]
```

For `body`:
```
[
  { raw: "2 sets of 4\" 150# spiral wound gaskets, 304 SS/graphite",
    description: "4\" 150# spiral wound gasket, 304 SS/graphite",
    qty: 2, uom: "SET" },
  ... 1 more
]
```

One call per document. `source` is the document's own name, so it's always right.

---

## Step 5 — Check every line

**IN:** the suggested lines + the text of the document they claim to come from

**OUT:** the lines that survive

```
44 suggested from the PDF  →  44 kept
 4 suggested from the body →   2 kept, 2 thrown away
```

The 2 thrown away were the gasket lines — the AI returned them *again* while reading the PDF, because it could see the body as background. The check asked: **are these words actually in the PDF?** No → dropped.

Four checks run here:

| check | throws away |
|---|---|
| is the line really in that document? | lines copied from somewhere else |
| is it a heading / total / price row? | `TOTAL QTY \| 35` |
| is the unit one of the 14 allowed? | → otherwise `null` |
| did they state a number at all? | `"a couple caps"` → qty `null` |

---

## Step 6 — Look at the whole inbox

**IN:** all 24 results, sorted by date

**OUT:** the links and the flag added

```
E008:  duplicate_of = "E006",  line_items = []     (same PDF, later date)
E004:  revises      = "E003",  line_items = [8 complete lines]
E017:  needs_review = true,    "refers to an attached list, none found"
E022:  needs_review = true,    "PDF is password protected"
```

This step needs the *other* emails, which is why it runs last and in date order.

---

## Final output

**IN:** everything above

**OUT:** `parsed.json`

```json
"E006": {
  "classification": "rfq",
  "revises": null,
  "duplicate_of": null,
  "needs_review": false,
  "review_reason": null,
  "line_items": [
    { "raw": "2 sets of 4\" 150# spiral wound gaskets, 304 SS/graphite",
      "description": "4\" 150# spiral wound gasket, 304 SS/graphite",
      "qty": 2, "uom": "SET", "source": "body" },
    { "raw": "1 | 7 | EA | 1/2\" | WELD NECK FLANGE, STD BORE",
      "description": "1/2\" weld neck flange, 150# RF, A105, STD bore",
      "qty": 7, "uom": "EA", "source": "RFQ_PF-26-3091.pdf" }
  ]
}
```

Plus `parsed.cost.json` — 58 calls, $0.2882, $0.0120 per email.

---

## The one-line version

```
bytes → record → documents → label → suggested lines → checked lines → linked & flagged → JSON
  1        2          3            4                5                    6
```

**Steps 1, 2, 5, 6 are plain code. Steps 3 and 4 are the AI.**
The AI only ever *reads*. Code decides what ships.

Look at the last two lines — that's the whole answer:

```
in key but NOT in ours : candidates, id, match, must_mention, must_not_mention, qty_tol, sku
in ours but NOT in key : description
```

**The answer key has no `description` field. We have no `must_mention` field.** That's not an accident — they're two sides of the same thing.

## Why

There is no single correct wording for a description. All of these are right:

```
"2\" pipe, SCH 40 A53B ERW, threaded & coupled"
"2 inch Schedule 40 A53B ERW pipe, T&C"
"PIPE 2\" SCH 40 A53B ERW T&C"
```

So the graders can't write down *the* answer. Instead they write down **the test**:

```json
"must_mention":     ["pipe", "sch 40|schedule 40", "a53b", "erw", "t&c|threaded and coupled|..."],
"must_not_mention": ["malleable", "150#"]
```

Which means: *"whatever words you use, it has to mention these, and must not mention those."*

**You write the answer. They write the test.**

If you output `must_mention` yourself, you'd be writing your own exam paper.

## What each extra field actually is

| field in the key | what it's for | do we output it? |
|---|---|---|
| `id` (`"E003-1"`) | their bookkeeping — names each key line | **no** |
| `qty_tol` | how strict to be on qty: `0` = exact, `null` = don't score | **no** |
| `must_mention` | the test your `description` has to pass | **no** |
| `must_not_mention` | the test it must not fail | **no** |
| `sku`, `match`, `candidates` | the answers for the **optional** matcher | **not yet** — see below |

The README says this directly:

> **`answer_key.json` fields beyond the schema:** `id`; `qty_tol`; `must_mention`; `must_not_mention`; `sku` / `match` / `candidates`

"Beyond the schema" = not part of what you produce.

## A concrete pair

Our output for E003 line 1:

```json
{ "raw": "1) 20 jts - 2\"",
  "description": "2\" pipe, SCH 40 A53B ERW, threaded & coupled",
  "qty": 20, "uom": "EA", "source": "body" }
```

Their key for the same line:

```json
{ "id": "E003-1", "raw": "1) 20 jts - 2\"", "qty": 20, "qty_tol": 0, "uom": "EA", "source": "body",
  "must_mention": ["pipe", "sch 40|schedule 40", "a53b", "erw", "t&c|threaded and coupled|..."],
  "must_not_mention": ["malleable", "150#"] }
```

Grading: pair the two on `raw` → check `qty` within `qty_tol` → check `uom` → check `source` → check the description contains every `must_mention` and no `must_not_mention`.


`check_format.py` is the authority on what you output, and it checks exactly five per line: `raw`, `description`, `qty`, `uom`, `source`. We produce exactly those five, and `check_format.py` reports **0 problems** on our `parsed.json`.

"""Stage 4 — extraction.  One model call per document (text or picture).

Per-document rather than per-email buys four things: `source` is right by
construction, a 300-page PDF cannot blow up one prompt, documents extract in
parallel, and a document that fails takes only itself down.

Every call also receives the email's subject and body as *ambient context*,
because context and quantity often live apart from the list — a photo of a
nameplate carries the specification while the body carries "quote 3 of these".
What keeps that from leaking into invented lines is not the prompt but the
groundedness check in verify.py.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from .llm import image_part, text_part
from .prompts import EXTRACT_IMAGE_SYSTEM, EXTRACT_TEXT_SYSTEM, REVISE_SYSTEM, ambient_context
from .schemas import EXTRACT_SCHEMA, REVISE_SCHEMA

MAX_DOC_CHARS = 60_000
CHUNK_CHARS = 18_000


def _chunks(text: str) -> list[str]:
    """Split a long document on blank lines / sheet breaks, never mid-row."""
    if len(text) <= CHUNK_CHARS:
        return [text]
    out, cur = [], []
    size = 0
    for line in text.splitlines(keepends=True):
        if size + len(line) > CHUNK_CHARS and cur:
            out.append("".join(cur))
            cur, size = [], 0
        cur.append(line)
        size += len(line)
    if cur:
        out.append("".join(cur))
    return out


def _extract_images(email, doc, ctx, runner, vision_model: str) -> dict:
    """One call per page; a tall page is shown as overlapping strips.

    Both choices exist for the same reason: the fewer rows a model looks at in one
    go, the less it drifts across them.  Keeping pages in separate calls also bounds
    the output length, so a twenty-page scan cannot truncate a single response.
    """
    from .documents import split_tall

    merged = {"document_role": "no_items", "notes": "", "unresolvable_reference": None, "lines": []}
    roles = []

    for page_no, page in enumerate(doc.images, start=1):
        strips = split_tall(page)
        where = doc.source if len(doc.images) == 1 else f"{doc.source}, page {page_no} of {len(doc.images)}"
        note = f"\n=== THE PICTURE: {where} ===\n"
        if len(strips) > 1:
            note += (
                f"This one page is supplied as {len(strips)} overlapping horizontal strips, top to "
                "bottom. They are parts of a single page, not separate documents, and the strips "
                "overlap — so a row near a strip's edge may appear twice. Return every item exactly "
                "once, and skip a row that is cut off at an edge if you cannot read it completely: "

            note += (

                + "\n".join(f"  {l.get('raw', '')}   ->   {l.get('description', '')}" for l in tail)
                + "\nIf this page continues that table, it continues its section too: carry the "
                "same heading and defaults onto these rows unless this page states otherwise, "
                "and do not repeat rows already listed above.\n"
            )

            email_id=email.id,
            model=vision_model,
            system=EXTRACT_IMAGE_SYSTEM,
            parts=parts,
            schema=EXTRACT_SCHEMA,
            schema_name="document_line_items",
            max_tokens=8000,
        )

        roles.append(res.get("document_role", "no_items"))
        merged["unresolvable_reference"] = merged["unresolvable_reference"] or res.get("unresolvable_reference")
        if res.get("notes"):
            merged["notes"] = (merged["notes"] + " " + res["notes"]).strip()

        merged["document_role"] = "item_list"

    elif roles and all(r == "unreadable" for r in roles):

    pieces = _chunks(text)

    """Apply a reply's changes to the earlier request and return the complete order."""

            f"{quoted or '(none)'}\n"

        model=model,
        system=REVISE_SYSTEM,

        schema_name="revised_order",

content.text:
## Answer to your question

**Before:** the whole PDF got one verdict. Any usable text layer → "this is a text document", and the pixels were never looked at. Your case lost every item inside the image.

**Now:** each page decides for itself, and a text page that also carries a big picture contributes both.

```
for each page:
    does this page have real text?
        YES → take the text
              + does it also hold a big embedded image?   (≥8% of the page, ≥200px)
                YES → take that image too
        NO  → it's a scan: render the page as a picture
```

Four possible outcomes for one PDF:

| pages | document kind | what gets read |
|---|---|---|
| all typed | `text` | text only — E006, E015 |
| all photographed | `image` | pictures only — E009 |
| typed + photographed pages | `mixed` | text from some pages, pictures from others |
| typed page with a screenshot in it | `mixed` | the text **and** the embedded picture |

### Why it can't double-count

The two halves read **disjoint parts of the file**. The text layer describes the typed words; the embedded image is a region the text layer says nothing about. So I extract the *image object itself* rather than re-rendering the whole page — if I rendered the page, a table that exists in both the text and the render would come back twice.

Each half is also verified against its own evidence: text-half lines must appear in the text layer; image-half lines can't be checked that way and are marked as such.

### Proof

Same hybrid PDF, run end to end:

```
before:  text = "Ridgeline RFQ - Job 4412... Needed 11/20... Terms net 30."
         line items: 0          ← the BOM was invisible

after:   kind = mixed, 1 embedded image
         line items: 6
           40  EA   1/2"-13 x 2" hex cap screw, Gr 5 zinc
           40  EA   1/2"-13 hex nut, zinc
           200 FT   1-5/8" strut channel, 12 ga, pre-galv
           3   BX   1/2" channel spring nuts, galv
           24  EA   2" pipe clamp, galv
           12  EA   3/4"-10 all-thread rod, 6 ft
```

### The part that actually worried me

If that had been the *only* failure mode it would have been survivable — zero items plus "you promised an attachment and none carried items" would have flagged it for a human.

But if the email body had carried two items of its own, we'd have shipped **2 lines instead of 8, with `needs_review: false`**. A partial order that looks like a successful parse. That's a silent loss dressed up as a clean result, and nothing downstream would ever have caught it.

Dev is unchanged (P/R still 100%, same 2202-char text for E006), so the committed cache stays valid.

Good question — that's the second real bug found by asking "what about an input shape the dev set doesn't contain," after the empty-email one the resilience test caught. Both came from thinking about input *shapes* rather than the 24 examples, which is exactly the thing that transfers to the 40.

"""Stage 4 — extraction.  One model call per document (text or picture).

Per-document rather than per-email buys four things: `source` is right by
construction, a 300-page PDF cannot blow up one prompt, documents extract in
parallel, and a document that fails takes only itself down.

Every call also receives the email's subject and body as *ambient context*,
because context and quantity often live apart from the list — a photo of a
nameplate carries the specification while the body carries "quote 3 of these".
What keeps that from leaking into invented lines is not the prompt but the
groundedness check in verify.py.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from .llm import image_part, text_part
from .prompts import EXTRACT_IMAGE_SYSTEM, EXTRACT_TEXT_SYSTEM, REVISE_SYSTEM, ambient_context
from .schemas import EXTRACT_SCHEMA, REVISE_SCHEMA

MAX_DOC_CHARS = 60_000
CHUNK_CHARS = 18_000


def _chunks(text: str) -> list[str]:
    """Split a long document on blank lines / sheet breaks, never mid-row."""
    if len(text) <= CHUNK_CHARS:
        return [text]
    out, cur = [], []
    size = 0
    for line in text.splitlines(keepends=True):
        if size + len(line) > CHUNK_CHARS and cur:
            out.append("".join(cur))
            cur, size = [], 0
        cur.append(line)
        size += len(line)
    if cur:
        out.append("".join(cur))
    return out


def _extract_images(email, doc, ctx, runner, vision_model: str) -> dict:
    """One call per page; a tall page is shown as overlapping strips.

    Both choices exist for the same reason: the fewer rows a model looks at in one
    go, the less it drifts across them.  Keeping pages in separate calls also bounds
    the output length, so a twenty-page scan cannot truncate a single response.
    """
    from .documents import split_tall

    merged = {"document_role": "no_items", "notes": "", "unresolvable_reference": None, "lines": []}
    roles = []

    for page_no, page in enumerate(doc.images, start=1):
        strips = split_tall(page)
        where = doc.source if len(doc.images) == 1 else f"{doc.source}, page {page_no} of {len(doc.images)}"
        note = f"\n=== THE PICTURE: {where} ===\n"
        if len(strips) > 1:
            note += (
                f"This one page is supplied as {len(strips)} overlapping horizontal strips, top to "
                "bottom. They are parts of a single page, not separate documents, and the strips "
                "overlap — so a row near a strip's edge may appear twice. Return every item exactly "
                "once, and skip a row that is cut off at an edge if you cannot read it completely: "
                "it is readable in full in the neighbouring strip.\n"
            )
        if merged["lines"]:
            # A table continued onto a new page keeps the section that was open when
            # the page broke — and that heading is back on the previous page, which
            # this call cannot see.  Hand over the tail of what has been read already.
            tail = merged["lines"][-4:]
            note += (
                "\nRows already read from earlier pages of this same document, oldest first:\n"
                + "\n".join(f"  {l.get('raw', '')}   ->   {l.get('description', '')}" for l in tail)
                + "\nIf this page continues that table, it continues its section too: carry the "
                "same heading and defaults onto these rows unless this page states otherwise, "
                "and do not repeat rows already listed above.\n"
            )

        parts = [text_part(ctx + note)]
        for s in strips:
            parts.append(image_part(s, "image/png" if len(strips) > 1 else doc.media_type))

        res = runner.complete_json(
            email_id=email.id,
            model=vision_model,
            system=EXTRACT_IMAGE_SYSTEM,
            parts=parts,
            schema=EXTRACT_SCHEMA,
            schema_name="document_line_items",
            max_tokens=8000,
        )
        merged["lines"].extend(res.get("lines") or [])
        roles.append(res.get("document_role", "no_items"))
        merged["unresolvable_reference"] = merged["unresolvable_reference"] or res.get("unresolvable_reference")
        if res.get("notes"):
            merged["notes"] = (merged["notes"] + " " + res["notes"]).strip()

    if "item_list" in roles:
        merged["document_role"] = "item_list"
    elif roles and all(r == "decorative" for r in roles):
        merged["document_role"] = "decorative"
    elif roles and all(r == "unreadable" for r in roles):
        merged["document_role"] = "unreadable"
    merged["_strip_split"] = True
    return merged


def extract_document(email, doc, documents, runner, *, text_model: str, vision_model: str) -> dict:
    """Return {document_role, lines[], notes, unresolvable_reference} for one document."""
    ctx = ambient_context(email, documents)

    if doc.kind == "image":
        return _extract_images(email, doc, ctx, runner, vision_model)

    if doc.kind == "mixed":
        # Both halves, merged.  They cover disjoint parts of the file — the text layer
        # and the pictures it does not describe — so neither can repeat the other.
        from_text = _extract_text(email, doc, ctx, runner, text_model)
        from_images = _extract_images(email, doc, ctx, runner, vision_model)
        for ln in from_text.get("lines") or []:
            ln["_from"] = "text"
        for ln in from_images.get("lines") or []:
            ln["_from"] = "image"
        roles = {from_text.get("document_role"), from_images.get("document_role")}
        return {
            "document_role": "item_list" if "item_list" in roles else "no_items",
            "notes": " ".join(x for x in (from_text.get("notes"), from_images.get("notes")) if x),
            "unresolvable_reference": from_text.get("unresolvable_reference")
            or from_images.get("unresolvable_reference"),
            "lines": (from_text.get("lines") or []) + (from_images.get("lines") or []),
            "_strip_split": from_images.get("_strip_split", False),
            "_mixed": True,
        }

    return _extract_text(email, doc, ctx, runner, text_model)


def _extract_text(email, doc, ctx, runner, text_model: str) -> dict:
    text = doc.text[:MAX_DOC_CHARS]
    pieces = _chunks(text)
    merged = {"document_role": "no_items", "notes": "", "unresolvable_reference": None, "lines": []}
    for i, piece in enumerate(pieces):
        label = doc.source if len(pieces) == 1 else f"{doc.source} (part {i + 1} of {len(pieces)})"
        head = ctx + f"\n=== THE DOCUMENT: {label} ===\n"
        if i and pieces[0]:
            # carry the document's own opening lines into later chunks: that is where
            # the sheet title and the "unless noted" defaults live
            head += "--- opening lines of this document, for context ---\n"
            head += "\n".join(pieces[0].splitlines()[:8]) + "\n--- continues ---\n"
        res = runner.complete_json(
            email_id=email.id,
            model=text_model,
            system=EXTRACT_TEXT_SYSTEM,
            parts=[text_part(head + piece)],

9	property of the system rather than a hope about a prompt.
10	"""

12	from __future__ import annotations
13	
14	from .ingest import normalised_body, normalised_subject
15	from .verify import tokens

18

32	    plus content equality by at least one of three independent routes.  Body text is

34	    attaching byte-identical files, so the attachment hashes do the real work.

40	    body = normalised_body(result.email.body_current)

42

54	            return prior

61	    """The earlier request this reply changes, if it is in this inbox."""
62	    email = result.email
63	    refs = f"{email.headers.get('in_reply_to') or ''} {email.headers.get('references') or ''}"
64	    subj = normalised_subject(email.subject)
65	
66	    by_header = [p for p in seen if p.email.headers.get("message_id") and p.email.headers["message_id"] in refs]

69	
70	    same_thread = [

84	    elsewhere.  Each reason below is a thing we could not read or could not resolve,
85	    never a thing we merely found hard.

90	        return

101	    item_docs = [d for d in result.documents if d.source != "body" and d.kind != "unreadable"]

105	    # scoped to that document.  If another document in the same email did supply the
106	    # items, the reference resolved — the email as a whole is complete.  Only a reference
107	    # that nothing in the email could satisfy is a reason to stop a quote.
108	    if result.unresolvable_reference and not carried_items:

118	            )

132	    seen: list = []
133	    for r in results:

135	        if dup is not None:
136	            r.duplicate_of = dup.id
137	            r.classification = dup.classification
138	            r.lines = []
139	        seen.append(r)

1	"""Stage 4 — extraction.  One model call per document (text or picture).
2	
3	Per-document rather than per-email buys four things: `source` is right by
4	construction, a 300-page PDF cannot blow up one prompt, documents extract in
5	parallel, and a document that fails takes only itself down.
6	
7	Every call also receives the email's subject and body as *ambient context*,
8	because context and quantity often live apart from the list — a photo of a
9	nameplate carries the specification while the body carries "quote 3 of these".
10	What keeps that from leaking into invented lines is not the prompt but the
11	groundedness check in verify.py.
12	"""
13	
14	from __future__ import annotations
15	
16	from .llm import image_part, text_part
17	from .prompts import EXTRACT_IMAGE_SYSTEM, EXTRACT_TEXT_SYSTEM, REVISE_SYSTEM, ambient_context
18	from .schemas import EXTRACT_SCHEMA, REVISE_SCHEMA
19	
20	CHUNK_CHARS = 18_000
21	CHUNK_ROWS = 120
22	
23	
24	def _chunks(text: str) -> list[str]:
25	    """Split a long document, never mid-row.
26	
27	    Bounded by ROWS as well as characters, because the binding constraint is the
28	    model's *output*: every row comes back as a raw, a description and its context,
29	    roughly 70 tokens. Six hundred rows in one call is a cheap-looking prompt and a
30	    40,000-token answer that gets cut off at the budget — and a truncated answer
31	    loses the whole document, not the tail of it.
32	    """
33	    lines = text.splitlines(keepends=True)
34	    if len(lines) <= CHUNK_ROWS and len(text) <= CHUNK_CHARS:
35	        return [text]
36	    out, cur, size = [], [], 0
37	    for line in lines:
38	        if cur and (len(cur) >= CHUNK_ROWS or size + len(line) > CHUNK_CHARS):
39	            out.append("".join(cur))
40	            cur, size = [], 0
41	        cur.append(line)
42	        size += len(line)
43	    if cur:
44	        out.append("".join(cur))
45	    return out
46	
47	
48	def _extract_images(email, doc, ctx, runner, vision_model: str) -> dict:
49	    """One call per page; a tall page is shown as overlapping strips.
50	
51	    Both choices exist for the same reason: the fewer rows a model looks at in one
52	    go, the less it drifts across them.  Keeping pages in separate calls also bounds
53	    the output length, so a twenty-page scan cannot truncate a single response.
54	    """
55	    from .documents import split_tall
56	
57	    merged = {"document_role": "no_items", "notes": "", "unresolvable_reference": None, "lines": []}
58	    roles = []
59	
60	    for page_no, page in enumerate(doc.images, start=1):
61	        strips = split_tall(page)
62	        where = doc.source if len(doc.images) == 1 else f"{doc.source}, page {page_no} of {len(doc.images)}"
63	        note = f"\n=== THE PICTURE: {where} ===\n"
64	        if len(strips) > 1:
65	            note += (
66	                f"This one page is supplied as {len(strips)} overlapping horizontal strips, top to "
67	                "bottom. They are parts of a single page, not separate documents, and the strips "
68	                "overlap — so a row near a strip's edge may appear twice. Return every item exactly "
69	                "once, and skip a row that is cut off at an edge if you cannot read it completely: "
70	                "it is readable in full in the neighbouring strip.\n"
71	            )
72	        if merged["lines"]:
73	            # A table continued onto a new page keeps the section that was open when
74	            # the page broke — and that heading is back on the previous page, which
75	            # this call cannot see.  Hand over the tail of what has been read already.
76	            tail = merged["lines"][-4:]
77	            note += (
78	                "\nRows already read from earlier pages of this same document, oldest first:\n"
79	                + "\n".join(f"  {l.get('raw', '')}   ->   {l.get('description', '')}" for l in tail)
80	                + "\nIf this page continues that table, it continues its section too: carry the "
81	                "same heading and defaults onto these rows unless this page states otherwise, "
82	                "and do not repeat rows already listed above.\n"
83	            )
84	
85	        parts = [text_part(ctx + note)]
86	        for s in strips:
87	            parts.append(image_part(s, "image/png" if len(strips) > 1 else doc.media_type))
88	
89	        res = runner.complete_json(
90	            email_id=email.id,
91	            model=vision_model,
92	            system=EXTRACT_IMAGE_SYSTEM,
93	            parts=parts,
94	            schema=EXTRACT_SCHEMA,
95	            schema_name="document_line_items",
96	            max_tokens=8000,
97	        )
98	        merged["lines"].extend(res.get("lines") or [])
99	        roles.append(res.get("document_role", "no_items"))
100	        merged["unresolvable_reference"] = merged["unresolvable_reference"] or res.get("unresolvable_reference")
101	        if res.get("notes"):
102	            merged["notes"] = (merged["notes"] + " " + res["notes"]).strip()
103	
104	    if "item_list" in roles:
105	        merged["document_role"] = "item_list"
106	    elif roles and all(r == "decorative" for r in roles):
107	        merged["document_role"] = "decorative"
108	    elif roles and all(r == "unreadable" for r in roles):
109	        merged["document_role"] = "unreadable"
110	    merged["_strip_split"] = True
111	    return merged

113	
114	def extract_document(email, doc, documents, runner, *, text_model: str, vision_model: str) -> dict:
115	    """Return {document_role, lines[], notes, unresolvable_reference} for one document."""
116	    ctx = ambient_context(email, documents)
117	
118	    if doc.kind == "image":
119	        return _extract_images(email, doc, ctx, runner, vision_model)
120	
121	    if doc.kind == "mixed":
122	        # Both halves, merged.  They cover disjoint parts of the file — the text layer

135	            or from_images.get("unresolvable_reference"),
136	            "lines": (from_text.get("lines") or []) + (from_images.get("lines") or []),
137	            "_strip_split": from_images.get("_strip_split", False),

141	    return _extract_text(email, doc, ctx, runner, text_model)

content.text:
## Answer: it was broken, now it isn't

**What happened before** (3,000-row sheet, measured):

```
rows in spreadsheet   3,000
rows reaching model   1,996       ← cut at 60,000 characters
rows silently dropped 1,008
truncated flag        False       ← nobody ever told
```

A third of the order gone, `needs_review: false`, output looking like a clean parse. Same silent-partial-loss shape as the hybrid PDF you asked about before.

There was a **second** problem hiding behind it: chunks were sized by *input* characters, ~500 rows each. But the binding constraint is the **output** — each row comes back as raw + description + context, roughly 70 tokens. 500 rows = a 35,000-token answer against a 12,000 budget. It gets cut off, and a cut-off answer loses the *whole* document, not its tail.

## What it does now

```
read the sheet
   │
   ├─ ≤ 800 rows?  →  read all of it
   └─ > 800 rows?  →  read 800, set truncated = true
                      → needs_review: "800 of 3,004 rows were read,
                                       the remaining 2,204 were not"
   │
split into chunks of 120 rows          ← bounded by OUTPUT, not input
   │
each chunk also gets the document's opening lines
   (the title and the "ALL FITTINGS SW 3000# UNLESS NOTED" default)
```

The cap number is arbitrary and configurable (`RFQ_MAX_DOC_ROWS`). **The flag is the point.**

## Proof on a 300-row sheet

```
rows in sheet : 300
lines out     : 300        needs_review = false
item numbers  : 1..300,  unique = 300,  gaps = []

  item   1: 3/4" 45 Elbow SW 3000# A105
  item 151: 45 Elbow, 3/4", SW 3000# A105
  item 300: 1/2" SW 3000# A105 90 Elbow      ← default survived to the last chunk

5 calls, $0.1952
```

That last line is the bit I actually cared about. The spec `SW 3000# A105` is written **once**, in row 2 of the sheet. Chunk 3 never sees row 2 — so each chunk is handed the document's opening lines, and item 300 still carries it.

## Cost shape

| sheet | chunks | calls | cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6 rows (E016 CSV) | 1 | 2 | $0.002 |
| 55 rows (E021) | 1 | 3 | $0.032 |
| 300 rows | 3 | 5 | $0.195 |
| 3,000 rows | 7 (capped) | 9 | ~$0.45 + **flagged** |

It scales roughly linearly, which is why the cap exists at all — otherwise one email could eat several dollars without anyone deciding it should.

## Dev is untouched

Every dev attachment is small — biggest is E006's PDF at 57 rows, E021's workbook at 55. All still 1 chunk, all identical prompts, so the committed cache still hits and dev stays at **P/R 100%**.

---

That's three bugs now found the same way — by asking *"what input shape does the dev set not contain?"* rather than by looking at the 24 examples:

1. empty email + corrupt attachment → classified `other`, unflaggable → silent loss
2. PDF with text **and** images → pixels never read
3. spreadsheet over ~2,000 rows → third of it dropped, no flag

All three are invisible on dev and all three are plausible in 40 unseen emails. Keep asking these — it's the highest-value thing we can do with the time left.

def read_eml(data: bytes, source: str) -> Document:
    """An attached message — a bounce's original, or a forwarded .eml.

    Rendered with its own envelope so the classifier can see *whose* message it is.
    A bounce carries our own outbound RFQ; those are not customer requests.
    """
    from .ingest import ingest_bytes

    try:
        inner = ingest_bytes(data, f"{source}:inner")
    except Exception as exc:
        return Document(source=source, kind="unreadable", error=f"attached message unreadable: {exc}")

    head = [
        f"From: {inner.headers.get('from')}",
        f"To: {inner.headers.get('to')}",
        f"Date: {inner.headers.get('date')}",
        f"Subject: {inner.headers.get('subject')}",
    ]
    text = "=== ATTACHED MESSAGE ===\n" + "\n".join(head) + "\n\n" + inner.body_current
    d = Document(source=source, kind="text", text=text.strip())
    d.meta.update(
        attached_message=True,
        inner_from=inner.sender_addr,
        inner_from_us=inner.from_us,
        inner_subject=inner.subject,
    )
    return d
