content.text:
That's the sharpest question you've asked, and the answer is: **we don't check it.** The UI was lying.

## What actually happens

```python
# rfq/pipeline.py
haystack = doc.text if doc.kind == "text" else None
```

For an image, `haystack` is `None`, and `verify.py` skips the grounding check entirely:

```python
hay = set(tokens(haystack)) if haystack is not None else None
...
if hay is not None:          # ← never true for a picture
    ok, cov = grounded(raw, hay)
```

So E023's line — `Halvorsen Valve Co. forged steel gate valve, model HV-800-FGS, size 2 IN, class 800 LB, NPT ends, body A105, trim 13CR` — **shipped on the model's reading alone.** Nothing verified that nameplate says what the model claims it says. The panel asserting otherwise was wrong.

## What the panel says now

```
VERIFICATION          nothing dropped     1 unverifiable

✓ checked against the source text — 0 lines
  Every one of these had to occur in the document it claims to come from.

✗ cannot be checked — 1 line from IMG_4417.jpg
  This came out of a picture. There is no text to compare a line against, so the
  groundedness check does not run on it and these lines ship on the model's
  reading alone. It is the one place a hallucination could still get through.

still applied to every line, whatever the source
  • the unit must be one of the fourteen the format allows, or null
  • a heading, a totals row or a price label is not an item
  • a line that states no number keeps a null quantity
  • the same row returned twice is removed
```

## The number, now measured

```
dev inbox: 164 of 210 lines verifiable · 46 not · 22% ship unverified
source: IMG_4172.jpeg · IMG_4417.jpg · Scan_RFQ_SC-4418.pdf · image002.png
```

`DECISIONS.md` named this gap but never sized it. It now carries the 22% figure, because "a known limitation" and "a fifth of my output" are different claims.

## How I'd close it

Ask the model for a **verbatim transcription** of the picture first, as a separate call, then ground the extracted lines against *that* text. It converts the picture into a checkable source. Costs one extra call per image — about $0.01 on the dev inbox — and the two readings disagreeing is itself a review signal.

Not built. It's the first item on "what's next".

**One more bug this surfaced:** E004 reported `0 of 8 lines checked`. A revision's lines are produced in phase B, and the summary was never recomputed after the merge — so it still held phase A's figures, from before those lines existed. Fixed; it now correctly reads 8 of 8.

4	> before I thought about it, and a block of my own private test data; both are redacted, and

7	## Setup
8	
9	**Claude Code** (CLI, Opus 5, 1M context) for all of it — one session, no subagents, no MCP
10	servers, no custom skills, **no `CLAUDE.md` or other instruction files**. Everything the agent
11	knew it read out of `ASSESSMENT.md`, `data/README.md`, the 24 `.eml` files and `answer_key.json`
12	at the start of the session.
13	
14	Deliberate. The failure mode I feared was an agent writing a parser for emails it had never
15	opened, so the first instruction was to read the whole package and explain the problem back to
16	me, and the second was to design the architecture in prose before any code. Both are in the
17	transcript ahead of the first file.
18	
19	The tooling that mattered is not an agent feature: `scripts/score.py`, written early,
20	implementing the brief's metrics in its stated order. After that, every change was judged by a
21	number rather than by whether the diff looked reasonable.
22	
23	## How I worked
24	
25	Deterministic layer first, verified with no model at all — all 24 emails ingested, every
26	attachment routed, the hidden sheet skipped, the encrypted PDF flagged — so that when model
27	answers arrived I knew the inputs were right. Then the scorer, then the model layer. From there
28	a loop: run, score, read the per-email diff, find the *cause* rather than patch the symptom, fix,
29	re-run. Five loops took dev from P 70.6% with 87 hallucinated lines to P/R 100% with none.
30	
31	I reviewed every diff, under two rules. A fix goes in the layer that owns the decision — vague
32	quantities became code in `verify.py`, not another sentence in a prompt. And no fix may name a
33	string from the dev set: rules describe phenomena, because the held-out inbox has the same
34	situations in different words.
35	
36	## Three moments
37	
38	**It was wrong, and the scorer caught it — `0d8363a`.** Splitting tall scans into overlapping
39	strips fixed the quantity errors, so the agent added de-duplication by item number to drop rows
40	appearing in two strips. The next score run showed recall had *fallen*: E010 lost
41	`40 | EA | 1/2"-13 hex nut, zinc`. That screenshot's first column is the quantity, not an item
42	number, and two rows legitimately want 40 of something — "duplicate item number" had deleted a
43	real line. The fix checks whether the leading numbers form a contiguous index first. I would not
44	have caught this reading the diff; a net-positive change hid a regression inside it.
45

47	obvious move was a bigger model. I made the agent measure instead: `gpt-5` scored 14/28 on that
48	page against `gpt-4.1`'s 13/28, while three overlapping strips scored 28/28. Row drift, not model
49	strength — the newer model would have cost more, risked the run on your key, and fixed nothing.
50	Later I was the one who assumed wrong: pinning temperature to 0 looks obviously right for
51	extraction, and on a workbook whose spec lives in its tab names context carried 0 of 54 lines at
52	temperature 0 and 54 of 54 at 1.0, twice each. Low temperature makes the model transcribe a row
53	instead of rewriting it self-contained — the entire task. Both measurements are code comments now.
54	
55	**It saved me real time — `3c114a3`.** I asked which recent fixes a test would actually catch
56	regressing. Three were covered; two had been verified by hand in a scratch directory and that
57	evidence was gone. Writing the test took minutes and immediately found a case neither of us had
58	considered: a CSV named `.xlsx` fell through to generic text, losing the column structure that
59	separates a heading from a row.

62	its first run: an email with an empty subject, empty body and one corrupt attachment comes back
63	`other`, and the format forbids `needs_review` on `other`, so it leaves with no lines and no
64	flag. A silent loss produced by following the spec — now a code override, and my disagreement
65	with the README.

1	# Decisions
2	
3	Dev inbox, 24 emails, regenerated by `rfq parse`:
4	
5	| | |
6	|---|---|
7	| silent losses · hallucinated · lost · phantom | **0 · 0 · 0 · 0** |
8	| classification | 24/24 |
9	| line items | P 100% · R 100% (210/210) |
10	| paired fields | uom · source · context carried 100% · **qty 99.1%** |
11	| `revises` / `duplicate_of` · `needs_review` | 100% / 100% · P 1.0 R 1.0 |
12	| cost | $0.2948 cold · $0.0123/email · $0.0000 and 0 calls on re-run |
13	
14	Treat those with suspicion: I iterated against this key. See *Predictions*.
15	
16	## The shape of it
17	
18	**Code decides everything checkable; the model decides only what requires reading; nothing the
19	model says ships without being verified against the source.**
20	
21	Code owns MIME, the current-vs-quoted split, routing attachments by magic bytes, hidden sheets,
22	text-layer-vs-scan, the uom vocabulary, de-duplication, duplicate and revision links, and every
23	`needs_review` rule. The model owns which of seven classes, which rows are items, and which
24	context belongs on which line — reading judgements no regex does.
25	
26	Between them sits the thing I'd defend first: **every line's `raw` must occur in the document it
27	claims to come from**, by token coverage not substring (a pasted spreadsheet splits one row
28	across three lines). Failures are dropped. It caught the model re-emitting the body's gasket
29	lines while reading E006's PDF; tightening the prompt removed the cause, so the current run
30	drops nothing on dev and the guard lives in `tests/test_documents.py` instead — a verification
31	layer with no live example is one I'd want more evidence for than I have.
32	
33	Second: **quoted history is excluded from what the model sees**, not labelled. E012 is a status
34	inquiry with a seven-line RFQ pasted underneath; none of it reaches the extractor.
35	
36	## Something in the data that surprised me
37	
38	I assumed I could tell a logo from a document by file size, and wrote the threshold before
39	looking. In E010 the company logo is **3,307 bytes** and the screenshot holding six real line
40	items is **4,295**. In E017 the logo is **5,288** — larger than both. Any threshold I'd have
41	picked silently deletes a customer's order, and E017 is exactly the email where losing the
42	attachment is the point. So every image goes to the vision model and `"decorative"` is an answer
43	it may give.
44	
45	The second surprise was mechanical. On E009's two-page phone scan, reading a whole page got
46	**13 of 28** quantities right; three overlapping strips of the same page got **28 of 28**. I
47	assumed a stronger model would fix it and tested that: `gpt-5` scored **14 of 28**. The failure
48	is row drift over a tall skewed table, not recognition.
49	
50	## Something in the README I disagree with
51	
52	> `needs_review` … Only for `rfq`, `rfq_revision` and `purchase_order`.
53	
54	This makes the flag unavailable exactly when it is most needed. My resilience test generates an
55	email with an empty subject, an empty body and one corrupt attachment. There is no evidence of
56	what it is; the model called it `other` — defensible — and the rule then forbids flagging it, so
57	it leaves with no lines and no flag. A textbook silent loss, the failure the same document ranks
58	as most expensive, produced by following the format.
59	
60	So when nothing could be read and the headers do not positively say machine-generated, code
61	overrides the class to `rfq` so the flag becomes legal, and flags it — choosing a possible
62	phantom request over a possible silent loss, on the brief's own asymmetry.
63	
64	Smaller: *"not items in quoted earlier messages"* is wrong on E020, where "go ahead with items 1,
65	2 and 4" names items existing **only** in the quoted quote. I kept the rule with three declared
66	exceptions, each detectable from the current message: selecting numbered items from history, our
67	own rep forwarding a customer, and a revision restating an order.
68	
69	## Predictions for the held-out inbox
70	
71	| | predicted |
72	|---|---|
73	| silent losses · hallucinated · lost/phantom | 0–1 · 0–4 · 0–2 |
74	| classification | 90–97% |
75	| line recall / precision | 95–99% / 96–99% |
76	| qty · context carried | 95–99% · 93–98% |
77	| `needs_review` recall | 0.85–1.0 |
78	
79	**The two kinds I expect to get wrong.** *Photographs and scans of dense tables* — two quantities
80	on E009 are still wrong, adjacent rows, 2 in 210 lines. Strips shrank that failure, not removed
81	it; a steeper angle or a table with no item-number column to anchor on brings it back. It shows
82	as a wrong `qty` rather than a missing line, which is the better way to be wrong.
83	
84	*Thread messages doing two things at once* — a message that chases a quote **and** changes it has
85	no right answer in a seven-label schema, and I will pick the wrong half. Same for a rep relaying
86	a customer's correction: `rfq` and `rfq_revision` are both defensible.
87	
88	I also predicted a PO accepting items by description would fail. I built it (`S011` in
89	`tests/test_shapes.py`) rather than leave it a guess, and it returns the right two lines. The
90	prediction was wrong; I leave the correction visible because an untested prediction and a tested
91	one are not the same kind of claim.
92	
93	## How this runs for real
94	
95	**3,000 emails/day by webhook.** The webhook writes raw bytes to object storage and pushes a job.
96	Workers run phase A, which already shares nothing between emails. Phase B needs its thread, so it
97	keys on a thread id and serialises per thread — the one piece that does not scale as written,
98	because `link_inbox` walks a list in memory. At $0.012 that is $36/day, and the classification
99	gate means the ~40% carrying no items costs a twentieth of it. **Built:** per-email isolation,
100	parallelism, cost accounting. **Not built:** the queue, the thread store.
101	
102	**Provider down two hours.** Four retries with backoff and jitter; past that the email returns
103	flagged and the run continues — a backlog of flagged emails, not a crash. Verified by running the
104	whole dev inbox with the key removed. **Missing:** a circuit breaker (every email pays its own
105	retries) and a requeue.
106	
107	**A 300-page PDF.** Capped at 20 pages, and a truncated document sets `needs_review` naming the
108	file. Text chunks at 120 rows — the binding constraint is *output*, ~70 tokens a row against a
109	12,000 budget. Oversized spreadsheets cap at 800 rows and say how many they did not read.
110	**Built**, though the cap is blunt; the right version prices the document and asks.
111	
112	**The same email twice.** Two mechanisms. The cache is content-addressed, so a second delivery
113	costs nothing. The duplicate rule then marks it: same sender, same subject once `Re:`/`FW:`/
114	`RESEND:` and trailing resend markers are stripped, plus content equality by attachment hash,
115	body, or extracted lines — or identical files where the message calls itself a resend. **Built.**
116	
117	## What I know is broken
118	
119	- Two quantities on E009's scan (adjacent rows in a photographed table).
120	- `verify.py` cannot ground a line from a picture — no text to check against. On dev that is
121	  **46 of 210 lines, 22%**. They get every other check, not the one asking whether the line
122	  exists. I'd close it with a verbatim transcription pass to ground against.
123	- `link_inbox` holds the inbox in memory.
124	- Temperature: I assumed pinning it to 0 could only help. On a workbook whose spec lives in tab
125	  names, context carried **0 of 54** lines at 0 and 0.2, and **54 of 54** at 1.0, twice each. Low
126	  temperature makes the model transcribe a row instead of rewriting it self-contained — the whole
127	  task. Pinned at 1.0, in the cache key. I have not found where between 0.2 and 1.0 it flips.
128	- The classifier's second-opinion escalation has never fired on real data.
129	
130	## What I rejected, and what's next
131	
132	Rejected: a stronger model instead of better framing (measured above); defaulting to `gpt-5.x`

I went back through the brief line by line. **I found one real problem, now fixed. Three things remain, all yours.**

## What was wrong

**Both write-ups were over the stated limits** — the brief says `DECISIONS.md` ≤ 2 pages and `AI_USAGE.md` ≤ 1 page. They'd grown to roughly **4 pages and 1.5**. That's the kind of thing a reviewer registers as not following instructions before reading a word of the content.

```
DECISIONS.md   2,346 → 1,420 words    all four required sections intact
AI_USAGE.md      857 →   717 words    three headings + commit hashes intact
```

Nothing of substance was cut — every number, every finding, the four required sections, the time figure.

## Everything else checks out

| | |
|---|---|
| Command shape | `parse --emails <dir> --out parsed.json` ✓ |
| Replayable with no key | ✓ verified from a fresh clone |
| Idempotent / free second run | ✓ 0 calls, $0.0000 |
| One bad email never kills the run | ✓ `tests/test_resilience.py` |
| You know what it cost | ✓ `parsed.cost.json`, per email |
| `RUNNING.md` · `parsed.json` · `DECISIONS.md` · `AI_USAGE.md` · `MATCHER.md` | ✓ |
| `ai-sessions/` | ✓ keys and private material redacted, verified |
| Commit history, unsquashed | ✓ 42 commits |
| Time stated | ✓ "roughly 9 hours" |
| OpenAI default path | ✓ `gpt-4.1-mini` / `gpt-4.1` |
| No outbound side effects | ✓ model provider only; UI binds loopback |
| Windows / Python 3.11+ | ✓ pure wheels, no shell, no POSIX deps |
| Under 50 MB | ✓ 9.7 MB |

Also checked and clean: `check_format.py` passes, all four test suites pass without a key, no API key anywhere tracked, and no Python 3.12-only syntax.

---

## Three things left, all yours

**1. The screen recording** ≤5 min → paste the link at `RUNNING.md:125` (the `TODO` marker is there). This is the only outright missing deliverable.

**2. Confirm "roughly 9 hours"** in `DECISIONS.md` — it's my estimate from the session, and the brief asks *you* to state it.

**3. Read `AI_USAGE.md` as your own words** and then run, last thing before you send:

```bash
python scripts/export_sessions.py && git add -A && git commit -m "final session export"
```

This conversation keeps growing, and the script redacts both keys and the private material automatically — it refuses to finish if either survives.

---

One thing worth deciding: the transcript carries a one-line marker where the private block was removed. It reveals nothing about the content, and I left it because an unexplained 368-entry gap in a log being read for integrity looks worse than a stated one. If you'd rather it be silent, say the word — it's a one-line change.

# Screen recording — 5 minutes

Not in the repo. Delete when you're done.

**Before you hit record**
- `rfq-ui` running at `http://127.0.0.1:8765`, dev emails already dropped and **processed**
  (so you're not watching a progress bar on camera), nothing expanded
- A second tab/window with `DECISIONS.md` open, in case you want to point at a number
- Browser zoomed so the eight columns fit without horizontal scrolling

Read it in your own words. The timings are a budget, not a script to recite.

---

## 0:00 – 0:40 · What the problem is

> "Ridgeline sells pipe and fittings. One inbox, `rfq@ridgeline-supply.example`, and all day
> customers email asking for prices. A rep opens each one and does two things: decides what kind
> of email it is, and writes down the items being asked for. That's the job I automated.
>
> It's hard because the emails are messy the way real ones are — a spreadsheet with the schedule
> in a heading above the rows, a phone photo of a handwritten list with one line crossed out, a
> bounce notification carrying our own outbound order, the same RFQ sent twice."

*Scroll the grid slowly once while you say this — 24 rows, no clicking.*

---

## 0:40 – 1:30 · The architecture

*Point at the diagram across the top.*

> "Six steps. Four are plain code, two call a model — blue and purple up here.
>
> Code opens the envelope and splits what they wrote now from the thread quoted below it. Code
> turns every attachment into either text or pictures. Then a model decides which of seven kinds
> of email it is. Then a model reads each document. Then **code** checks every line the model
> returned. Then code places it in the inbox — duplicate, revision, needs a human.
>
> One sentence explains all of it: **the model only ever reads. Code decides what ships.** The
> model is good at 'which words on this page belong to this line' — no regex does that. It is
> not trusted with 'does this line exist', 'is EA a valid unit', 'is this a duplicate'. Those are

Here's the architecture narration to follow straight on from your opening. Stage directions in *italics*, the words in plain text.

---

## Step by step — the architecture

*Point at the diagram across the top of the page.*

> Every email goes through six steps. **Four are plain code, two call a model** — that's the blue and the purple up here. The order matters, so let me walk it.

---

**① Open the envelope** — *point at box 1*

> First, pure code. Unpack the email, pull out who sent it, the subject, the date, the body, the attachments.
>
> And then the one thing that matters most in the whole pipeline: **split what they wrote now from the thread quoted underneath it.** A reply to last week's email has last week's order sitting below it. That old order was already handled. If it reaches the model, you quote it twice.

---

**② Read the attachments** — *point at box 2*

> Still code, no AI. Every attachment becomes one of two things: **text, or pictures.**
>
> An Excel file becomes text — and we skip hidden sheets, because a hidden tab is the customer telling you it's not the live version. Word, CSV, the same. A PDF we test for a real text layer: if it has one we rebuild the table columns from the word positions; if it doesn't, it's a scan, so we render the pages as images.
>
> And if we genuinely can't open something — a password-protected PDF, a corrupt file — **that is also an answer.** It gets recorded as "could not be read", which matters later.

---

**③ What kind of email is this?** — *point at box 3, the first purple one*

> Now the first model call. Seven kinds: a request for a quote, a revision of one, a purchase order, a supplier quoting *us*, someone chasing an existing quote, an auto-reply, or anything else.
>
> This is the hardest one to get right, because plenty of things **look** like a request and aren't. A supplier's quote is a neat list of items with quantities. A bounce notification carries our own outbound order inside it. A marketing blast is a price list. None of those are a customer asking for anything.

*Point at the gate line underneath the diagram.*

> And this step is a **gate**. Four of those seven kinds carry no items at all — so for those emails, we stop here. That's a deliberate cost decision, and you'll see it in the numbers in a minute.

---

**④ Read each document** — *point at box 4*

> The second model call — and it's **one call per document**, not one per email.
>
> So an email with a covering note and a PDF gets two calls. The job on each one is: which rows are actually items, and what context belongs on each of them. Because the spec is almost never on the line itself — it's in a heading above it, a sheet tab name, a form field at the top of the page.
>
> One call per document buys three things: the source filename is right automatically, a 300-page PDF can't blow up a single prompt, and if one attachment fails it takes only itself down.

---

**⑤ Check every line** — *point at box 5*

> Back to code. And this is the part I'd defend hardest.
>
> **The model's answer is treated as evidence, not truth.** Every line it returned has to actually occur in the document it claims to come from — if the words aren't there, the line is dropped before it ships. The unit has to be one of fourteen allowed values. A headings row, a totals row, a price label is not an item. And if the customer never stated a number, the quantity stays empty rather than being guessed.

---

**⑥ Place it in the inbox** — *point at box 6*

> Last step, code again, and it's the only one that looks at the **other** emails.
>
> Is this a duplicate of something already received? Is it a revision of an earlier request — and if so, what's the complete order now? And the one that matters most: **was there anything here we couldn't read?** If so it gets flagged for a human, with the reason.

---

**The principle** — *step back from the diagram*

> If you take one thing from the architecture, it's this: **the model only ever reads. Code decides what ships.**
>
> The model is good at "which words on this page belong to this line" — no amount of regex does that. But it is never trusted with anything checkable: does this line exist, is this a real unit, is this a duplicate, does a human need to look. Those are all code, because they can be verified.

---

> That's the design. Let me show you it actually running.

*Now move into the grid.*

---

### Two optional lines if you have room

Drop in after ③ if you want the cost point early:

> That gate is the difference between a tenth of a cent and four cents for a single email.

Drop in after ⑤ if you want to pre-empt the obvious question:

> And when it can't check — a line read off a photograph has no text to compare against — the system says so rather than pretending it verified it.

---

**Timing:** about 1:45 read at a normal pace. If you're tight, cut the three bullets explaining *why* one call per document, and the examples in ②.

# Ridgeline RFQ inbox reader

Reads an inbox of `.eml` files the way an inside sales rep does: decides what kind of email each
one is, and pulls out the line items being asked for — each one self-contained, with the
schedule, material or rating the customer wrote somewhere *other* than on that line.

```bash
python -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -e .
rfq parse --emails data/dev/emails --out parsed.json
```

**It runs with no API key.** Every model answer is recorded in `cache/` and committed, so the
dev inbox replays in under a second for $0.00 and produces byte-identical output.

## Results on the dev inbox

| | |
|---|---|
| silent losses · hallucinated lines · lost · phantom | **0 · 0 · 0 · 0** |
| classification | 24 / 24 |
| line items | precision 100% · recall 100% (210/210) |
| paired fields | uom · source · context carried 100% · qty 99.1% |
| `revises` / `duplicate_of` · `needs_review` | 100% / 100% · P 1.0 R 1.0 |
| cost | $0.2948 cold · $0.012 per email · **$0.0000** on re-run |

Those are measured by `scripts/score.py`, which implements the brief's metrics in the order it
says it grades them. They should be read with suspicion — see *Predictions* in `DECISIONS.md`.

## How it works

Six steps. Four are plain code, two call a model.

```
.eml → ① open the envelope   split the current message from the thread below it   code
     → ② read attachments    Excel · Word · CSV · PDF · photos → text or pictures  code
     → ③ what kind of email  one of seven — and a gate                            MODEL
     → ④ read each document  one call per document                                MODEL
     → ⑤ check every line    is it really in the document it claims?              code
     → ⑥ place in the inbox  duplicate · revision · needs review                   code
     → parsed.json
```

**The model only ever reads. Code decides what ships.** The model is good at *which words on
this page belong to this line* — no regex does that. It is never trusted with anything
checkable: whether a line exists, whether a unit is valid, whether an email is a duplicate,
whether a human needs to look. Those are code.

Step ③ is also a cost gate: four of the seven classes carry no line items, so those emails stop
there and cost $0.0007 instead of $0.03.

## The viewer

A local page that runs the same pipeline and shows every stage — including the exact prompt
sent to the model and the answer that came back.

```bash
rfq-ui                      # or: python ui/server.py
```

Opens `http://127.0.0.1:8765`, loopback only. **Drop `.eml` files on the page** — all at once or
a few at a time — then press **Process**. Dropping only reads the headers; nothing is sent
anywhere until you press it. Try `data/dev/emails/`; it replays from the committed cache, so it
returns in about a second and costs nothing.

The six stages are the columns and every email is a row, grouped by customer with revisions and
duplicates nested under the request they belong to. Each cell opens the thing it describes:

| column | what `view ›` opens |
|---|---|
| The email, as is | the message as it arrived, thread history greyed out beneath it |
| What code made of it | the record step ① built, the text kept, the text cut away, the header signals |
| Attachments | each file, how it routed, rendered images, the text the model is given — and a download |
| Classification | that model call in full: system prompt, user message, the JSON back |
| Model reads documents | one such card per document, with the strip images for a scan |
| Check every line | what was dropped and why, what could not be checked, what survived |
| Outcome | the final record, the lines a rep would quote, and what the email cost |

A **live calls** switch in the header ignores the recorded answers and calls the model for real.
It never writes to the cache, so experimenting cannot disturb the committed replay.

Three worth clicking: **E012** (a seven-line RFQ quoted under a status question, greyed out and
never shown to the model), **E011** (step ④ reads `skipped` — the gate, $0.0007), and **E009**
(a two-page phone scan, with the overlapping strips that are actually sent).

## Where everything is

| | |
|---|---|
| `RUNNING.md` | setup, the models, what a run costs, how to verify each property |
| `DECISIONS.md` | the design memo — the four sections the brief asks for |
| `MATCHER.md` | the optional catalog matcher, designed and not built |
| `AI_USAGE.md` · `ai-sessions/` | how the coding agent was directed, and the raw transcript |
| `rfq/` | the pipeline — one module per stage |
| `ui/` | the viewer. Reads the pipeline's output; never writes to it |
| `cache/` | recorded model answers. This is what makes the keyless replay work |
| `tests/` | four suites; three need no API key |
| `scripts/score.py` | the grader |

```bash
python scripts/score.py parsed.json data/dev/answer_key.json
python data/check_format.py parsed.json --emails data/dev/emails
python tests/test_documents.py      # and test_quoted_split, test_resilience
```

## A note on `data/` and `ASSESSMENT.md`

Those are the assessor's own material — the brief, the dev inbox and its answer key — kept in
the repo so the command and the scorer run straight from a clone. **This repository should stay
private for that reason.**

content.text:
## The problem, precisely

An email arrives. Something has to decide **what it is** and **what's being asked for**. Both answers have to be right, and both can be wrong in ways that cost money:

- Decide wrong and a customer never hears back — or a supplier's quote becomes a fake order.
- Extract wrong and you quote the wrong part at the wrong price.

What makes it hard isn't the reading. It's that **the information is never where the line is.** A row says `12 | EA | 6" | 90 LR elbow`. Whether that's a $9 carbon elbow or a $90 stainless one depends on a note three rows above it, or the name of the spreadsheet tab, or the subject line.

So the task is: pull a fact down from wherever it was written, onto the right lines, and **not onto the wrong ones**.

---

## The one principle

> **Code decides everything checkable. The model decides only what requires reading. Nothing the model says ships without being verified against the source.**

Every structural choice falls out of that sentence.

The reasoning: an LLM is genuinely good at *"which words on this page belong to this line"* — that's judgement about meaning, and no regex does it. But it's a terrible place to put *"does this line exist"*, *"is `EA` a valid unit"*, *"is this email a duplicate"*, *"should a human look at this"*. Those are all **verifiable**, which means code can answer them with certainty, and certainty beats a good guess every time.

The practical consequence is that the model is never the last word on anything. It produces *candidates*; code decides what ships.

---

## The pipeline, and why each stage exists

### ① Open the envelope — code

Parse MIME, pull headers and body, unpack attachments. Then the single highest-leverage thing in the system: **split what they wrote now from the thread quoted beneath it.**

Why it earns first place: E012 is a one-line question — *"any update on the quote?"* — with a complete seven-line RFQ pasted underneath from three weeks ago. That order was handled when it arrived. If it reaches the model, you quote it twice.

The design decision isn't "detect the quoted part and label it `ignore this`". It's **don't include it at all**. A label is an instruction the model can disobey; absence isn't. The model cannot hallucinate what it never saw.

Three narrow exceptions, each detectable from the current message alone: a message selecting numbered items from history (*"go ahead with 1, 2 and 4"*), our own rep forwarding a customer, and a revision restating an order.

### ② Read the attachments — code

Everything becomes one of two things: **text, or pictures.**

Routing is by **magic bytes, not filename** — exports are routinely misnamed, and a CSV read as prose loses the column structure that separates a heading from a row.

Three rules here are about *phenomena*, which is why they transfer:
- **Skip hidden spreadsheet tabs.** A hidden tab is the author saying "this isn't the live version". E005 hides `Rev A (old)` with different quantities behind the Rev B everyone is meant to read.
- **Test the PDF for a real text layer.** Has one → rebuild columns from word positions. Doesn't → it's a scan, render to images.
- **Never judge an image by its size.** E010's logo is 3,307 bytes; the screenshot holding six real line items is 4,295. E017's logo is 5,288 — bigger than both. Any threshold silently deletes an order.

And critically: **"I can't open this" is an answer, not a failure.** An encrypted PDF gets recorded as unreadable, which matters two stages later.

Because a Document carries its own filename, `source` on every extracted line is **correct by construction** — never a thing the model has to remember.

### ③ What kind of email — model, and a gate

Seven classes. Code hands over hard header signals first (bounce envelope, our own domain, `List-Unsubscribe`), and code can veto: a delivery-status envelope is `auto_reply` no matter what the model says, which is how E013's bounce — carrying our own outbound four-item order — never becomes a request.

**This is also a cost gate.** Four of the seven classes carry no items by definition, so those emails stop here. That's not a micro-optimisation: it's the difference between **$0.0007 and $0.03** per email, a 50× spread.

But a gate is dangerous — a misclassification here is a *silent loss*, the worst failure. So two guards: the prompt states the asymmetry explicitly (when torn, choose the class that carries items), and code double-checks — if the class says "no items" but the attachments contain a table with ≥3 quantity-bearing rows, code and model disagree and it escalates rather than silently returning `[]`.

### ④ Read each document — model, one call per document

Not one call per email. Four reasons:

- `source` is right automatically
- a 300-page PDF can't blow up a single prompt
- documents extract in parallel
- a failing document takes only itself down

But pure per-document breaks on E023 — the **quantity is in the body** (*"quote 3 of these"*) and the **spec is on a nameplate in a photo**. So every call also gets the subject and body as *ambient context*, with one hard rule: emit only lines that appear in **this** document.

That rule is enforced in code, not trusted to the prompt. **Ambient context in, strict source grounding out.**

The prompt itself describes *phenomena*, never dev-set strings: headings scope downward until the next heading of equal rank; a line stating its own value overrides an inherited default; ditto marks resolve from the line above; struck-through rows are deletions; totals and prices are not items; a vague quantity is `null`.

### ⑤ Check every line — code

Where precision is actually won. The model's answer is **evidence**:

| check | kills |
|---|---|
| does `raw` occur in that document? (token coverage) | lines lifted from elsewhere or invented |
| is this a heading / total / price label? | `TOTAL QTY \| 35` |
| is `uom` one of the fourteen? | anything else → `null` |
| did they state a number at all? | *"a couple caps"* → `null`, not 2 |
| is this row genuinely a repeat? | key includes the description, because GATE and CHECK sections can print identical rows |

This caught the model re-emitting the body's gasket lines while reading E006's PDF — it could see them in the ambient context. Code asked *"are those words in the PDF?"*, they weren't, and they were dropped.

**The honest limit:** a line read off a photograph has no text to compare against, so this check *doesn't run* on it. On dev that's 46 of 210 lines — 22% — shipping on the model's reading alone. The system says so rather than pretending otherwise.

### ⑥ Place it in the inbox — code

The only stage that looks at the *other* emails, so it runs last, **in Date order** — because the spec defines the duplicate as the later one, and a revision always follows its original.

- **Duplicate:** same sender + content equality by attachment hash, body, or extracted lines — or identical files where the message calls itself a resend.
- **Revision:** hand the model the earlier email's recorded lines plus the delta, get back the complete order.
- **`needs_review`:** a set of **code rules**, not a model opinion. A promised attachment that isn't there; a file that wouldn't open; items identified by something outside the email; zero lines on an item-class email; a cache miss with no key.

That last table is what makes *"no silent losses"* a **structural property** rather than a hope about a prompt.

---

## Underneath: three cross-cutting layers

**Content-addressed cache.** Key = hash of model + prompt version + temperature + rendered prompt + image bytes. Not the filename — a filename says nothing about content. One mechanism delivers both required properties: *replayable with no key* and *free on re-run*. Edit a prompt and every answer that used it correctly invalidates.

**Error boundary per email.** Any failure becomes a flagged record and the loop continues. The provider being down for two hours produces a backlog of flagged emails, not a crash and not an empty file.

**Cost ledger.** Every call is counted, priced and attributed. Cached answers carry the usage they were first recorded with, so a replay still reports what the inbox costs *cold* instead of a misleading $0.00.

---

## Why this shape survives emails I've never seen

Because nothing in it is keyed to a string from the dev set. Every rule is about a **phenomenon**:

| not this | but this |
|---|---|
| ignore the sheet named `Rev A (old)` | ignore hidden sheets and superseded revisions |
| E013 is a bounce | report envelope + attached message from us → never extract from it |
| E017's attachment is a logo | content decides what an image is; a promised-but-missing document is always a flag |
| E020 wants items 1, 2, 4 | a message selecting numbered items may read the block it selects from |

And three invariants hold whatever arrives: **every email appears in the output; every shipped line exists in a source document; anything unreadable is flagged, never dropped.**

---

## The two things I'd defend first in the interview

1. **Quoted history is excluded, not labelled.** The cheapest, most effective guard in the system has no AI in it at all.
2. **Code verifies what the model says.** Precision is a property of the architecture, not a hope about prompt wording — and where it *can't* verify (photographs), the system says so instead of claiming it did.
